def _get_inertia_and_budget_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    MIMOSA allows several types of constraints on emissions: a global carbon budget, inertia constraints,
    limits on net negative emissions and constraints on emissions after 2100.

    ## Carbon budget

    By default, the carbon budget is set to `False`, which means that MIMOSA runs in CBA mode without carbon budget.
    If a carbon budget is defined using the parameter [`carbonbudget`](#param__emissions.carbonbudget), the following constraint is active:

    $$
    \href{./#var__global_cumulative_emissions}{\text{cumulative emissions}_{t}} - \href{./#param__emissions.carbonbudget}{\text{budget}} \leq 0,
    $$

    for $t \geq 2100$. Note that the [`carbonbudget`](#param__emissions.carbonbudget) parameter unit should be
    in GtCO<sub>2</sub> (or TtCO<sub>2</sub> or MtCO<sub>2</sub>).

    ## Inertia

    In MIMOSA, there is a limit on how fast emissions can be reduced. This constraint is called inertia, and represents the
    technological, social, political and economic difficulties of quickly reducing emissions. It is implemented as a hard limit
    on the speed of emission reductions. The parameters [`inertia_global`](#param__emissions.inertia.global) and
    [`inertia_regional`](#param__emissions.inertia.regional) are defined as percentages of baseline emissions in the
    initial year. If baseline emissions in a region are 10 GtCO<sub>2</sub>/yr in the initial year, and the global inertia is 5%,
    then the global emissions cannot be reduced by more than 0.5 GtCO<sub>2</sub>/yr throughout the whole run. This way, the parameter
    is independent of the size of the region.

    === "Global inertia"


        $$
        \href{./#var__global_emissions}{\text{global emissions}_{t}} - \href{./#var__global_emissions}{\text{global emissions}_{t-1}} \geq \Delta t \cdot \href{./#param__emissions.inertia.global}{\text{inertia_global}} \cdot \text{scaling factor},
        $$

        with the scaling factor the global baseline emissions in the starting year:

        $$
        \text{scaling factor} = \left( \sum_r \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t=0,r}}\right)
        $$

        By default, the [`inertia_global`](#param__emissions.inertia.global) is set to `False`, such that there is no global inertia
        constraint. The only inertia constraint happens regionally by default.

    === "Regional inertia"

        $$
        \href{./#var__regional_emissions}{\text{regional emissions}_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__regional_emissions}{\text{regional emissions}_{t-1,r}} \geq \Delta t \cdot \href{./#param__emissions.inertia.regional}{\text{inertia_regional}} \cdot \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t=0,r}}.
        $$

        By default, the [`inertia_regional`](#param__emissions.inertia.regional) parameter is active, such that regional emissions cannot be reduced by more than 5% of the initial baseline emissions per year. This is
        based on maximum reduction speeds in scenarios underpinning the IPCC Special Report on Global Warming
        of 1.5°C, as analysed by [Hof et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fclim.2021.785577).


    ## Minimum emission levels (limits to net-negative emissions)

    Since the Marginal Abatement Cost curve is a continuous function with no upper bound, reductions can theoretically be without bound.
    To still address the difficulties associated with CDR technologies, a limit on (net) negative emissions can be imposed. These difficulties
    can be economic (e.g., land becoming increasingly scarce or increased dependence on expensive storage sites) or socio-political
    (e.g., concerns about biodiversity and food security). These restrictions and side effects are discussed by
    [Hof et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fclim.2021.785577) and
    [Fuss et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aabf9f). By default, global emissions
    are limited to -20 GtCO<sub>2</sub>/yr, and regional emissions to -10 GtCO<sub>2</sub>/yr:

    $$
    \href{./#var__global_emissions}{\text{global emissions}_t} \geq \href{./#param__emissions.global%20min%20level}{\text{global min level}},
    $$

    $$
    \href{./#var__regional_emissions}{\text{regional emissions}_t} \geq \href{./#param__emissions.regional%20min%20level}{\text{regional min level}}.
    $$

    Note that currently, the minimum regional emission level is the same for every region, but this could be easily changed if needed (see
    [Extending MIMOSA](../extending/index.md)).

    ## Constraints on emissions after 2100

    In CBA mode, it can be useful to run MIMOSA until 2150 instead of 2100, to avoid end-of-horizon effects. One way to mitigate
    this effect is to impose a constraint on the growth of emissions after 2100. By default, emissions are not allowed to grow after 2100:

    $$
    \href{./#var__regional_emissions}{\text{regional emissions}_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__regional_emissions}{\text{regional emissions}_{t-1,r}} \leq 0, \text{if } t - 1 > 2100,
    $$

    if the parameter [`non_increasing_emissions_after_2100`](#param__emissions.non%20increasing%20emissions%20after%202100) is set to `True`.

    When a carbon budget is imposed, it is also possible to impose a net-zero emissions constraint after the budget year (2100):

    $$
    \href{./#var__global_emissions}{\text{global emissions}_{t}} \leq 0, \text{if } t \geq 2100,
    $$
    if the parameter [`no_pos_emissions_after_budget_year`](#param__emissions.not%20positive%20after%20budget%20year) is set to `True`,
    **and** if a carbon budget is specified. Otherwise, this constraint is ignored.


    ## Parameters defined in this module
    - params["emissions"]["carbonbudget"]: Value of the carbon budget. Example: "800 GtCO2" (the unit is important). If set to False, no carbon budget is imposed: this is cost-benefit mode. Default: False.. Type: quantity. Default: False. Can also be false. Unit: emissions_unit.
    - params["emissions"]["inertia"]["global"]: Maximum reduction speed, in % of initial emissions (should be negative) Can also be false, then no inertia limit is imposed. Type: float. Default: False. Can also be false. Min: -inf. Max: 0.
    - params["emissions"]["inertia"]["regional"]: Maximum reduction speed, in % of initial emissions (should be negative) Can also be false, then no inertia limit is imposed. Type: float. Default: -0.05. Can also be false. Min: -inf. Max: 0.
    - params["emissions"]["global min level"]: Limit on the emission level (globally), mostly used for negative emissions. Can also be false, then no limit is imposed. Type: quantity. Default: -20 GtCO2/yr. Can also be false. Unit: emissionsrate_unit.
    - params["emissions"]["regional min level"]: Limit on the emission level (per region), mostly used for negative emissions. Can also be false, then no limit is imposed. Type: quantity. Default: -10 GtCO2/yr. Can also be false. Unit: emissionsrate_unit.
    - params["emissions"]["not positive after budget year"]: If true, impose net-zero emissions after budget year (2100). Type: bool. Default: True.
    - params["emissions"]["non increasing emissions after 2100"]: If true, the regional emissions after 2100 are not allowed to climb.. Type: bool. Default: True.

    """

    constraints = []

    m.budget = Param(initialize=inputs.config("emissions.carbonbudget"))
    m.inertia_global = Param(initialize=inputs.config("emissions.inertia.global"))
    m.inertia_regional = Param(initialize=inputs.config("emissions.inertia.regional"))
    m.global_min_level = Param(initialize=inputs.config("emissions.global min level"))
    m.regional_min_level = Param(
        initialize=inputs.config("emissions.regional min level")
    )
    m.non_increasing_emissions_after_2100 = Param(
        initialize=inputs.config("emissions.non increasing emissions after 2100")
    )
    m.no_pos_emissions_after_budget_year = Param(
        initialize=inputs.config("emissions.not positive after budget year")
    )
    constraints.extend(
        [
            # Carbon budget constraints:
            GlobalConstraint(
                lambda m, t: (
                    m.global_cumulative_emissions[t]
                    - (
                        m.budget
                        + (
                            m.overshoot[t] * (1 - m.perc_reversible_damages)
                            if value(m.perc_reversible_damages) < 1
                            else 0
                        )
                    )
                    <= 0
                    if (m.year(t) >= 2100 and value(m.budget) is not False)
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                name="carbon_budget",
            ),
            GlobalConstraint(lambda m, t: m.global_cumulative_emissions[t] >= 0),
            # Global and regional inertia constraints:
            GlobalConstraint(
                lambda m, t: (
                    m.global_emissions[t] - m.global_emissions[t - 1]
                    >= m.period_length[t]
                    * m.inertia_global
                    * sum(m.ssp_baseline_emissions[0, r] for r in m.regions)
                    if value(m.inertia_global) is not False and t > 0
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                name="global_inertia",
            ),
            # Regional inertia (skipped for when mitigation is delayed, since there is no mitigation in that period)
            RegionalConstraint(
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.regional_emissions[t, r] - m.regional_emissions[t - 1, r]
                    >= m.period_length[t]
                    * m.inertia_regional
                    * m.ssp_baseline_emissions[0, r]
                    if value(m.inertia_regional) is not False
                    and t > 0
                    and (
                        value(m.delay_mitigation_year) is False
                        or m.year(t) >= m.delay_mitigation_year
                    )
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                name="regional_inertia",
            ),
            GlobalConstraint(
                lambda m, t: (
                    m.global_emissions[t] >= m.global_min_level
                    if value(m.global_min_level) is not False
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                "global_min_level",
            ),
            RegionalConstraint(
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.regional_emissions[t, r] >= m.regional_min_level
                    if value(m.regional_min_level) is not False
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                "regional_min_level",
            ),
            RegionalConstraint(
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.regional_emissions[t, r] - m.regional_emissions[t - 1, r] <= 0
                    if t > 0
                    and m.year(t - 1) > 2100
                    and value(m.non_increasing_emissions_after_2100)
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                name="non_increasing_emissions_after_2100",
            ),
            GlobalConstraint(
                lambda m, t: (
                    m.global_emissions[t] <= 0
                    if (
                        m.year(t) >= 2100
                        and value(m.no_pos_emissions_after_budget_year) is True
                        and value(m.budget) is not False
                    )
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                name="net_zero_after_2100",
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: Emission trading
docs.text:
Back to general structure

Without emission trading, the reductions and mitigation costs attributed to a region are the reductions and costs that physically occur within that region. Emission trading allows this attribution to differ, for example because reductions are cheaper elsewhere or because an effort-sharing regime assigns a different distribution of emission allowances.

The emission trading module can be chosen using the parameter emissiontrade module.

docs.title: Physical and attributed reductions and costs
docs.text:
Emission trading distinguishes between where an emission reduction takes place and the region to which the reduction and its cost are attributed:

  • regional_emission_reductions is the physical reduction within a region.
  • attributed_emission_reductions is the reduction attributed to a region after trading.
  • domestic_mitigation_costs_abs is the cost of the physical reductions within a region.
  • mitigation_costs_abs is the cost attributed to a region after trading.

With emission trading, the two pairs are connected through the trading balances:

\[ \begin{align} \href{./#var__attributed_emission_reductions}{\text{attributed emission reductions}_{t,r}} &= \href{./#var__regional_emission_reductions}{\text{regional emission reductions}_{t,r}} + \href{./#var__emission_reduction_trading_balance}{\text{emission reduction trading balance}_{t,r}},\\ \href{./#var__mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} &= \href{./#var__domestic_mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{domestic mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} + \href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}}. \end{align} \]

A positive trading balance means that a region buys reductions and pays other regions. A negative balance means that a region sells reductions and receives payment. Without emission trading, both balances are zero, so physical and attributed reductions and costs are the same.

docs.title: Variables in the model results
docs.text:
Variable Meaning Unit Availability regional_emission_reductions Physical emission reduction within the region Emissions per year Both options attributed_emission_reductions Emission reductions attributed to the region after trading Emissions per year Emission trading only emission_reduction_trading_balance Reductions bought (positive) or sold (negative) by the region Emissions per year Both options; always zero without trade regional_emission_allowances Emissions assigned to the region after accounting for its attributed reductions Emissions per year Both options domestic_mitigation_costs_abs Cost of reductions taking place within the region Currency per year Both options mitigation_costs_abs Mitigation costs attributed to the region after trading Currency per year Both options mitigation_cost_trading_balance Payments made (positive) or received (negative) by the region Currency per year Both options; always zero without trade carbon_price Marginal carbon price in a region Currency per unit of emissions Both options global_carbon_price Population-weighted average carbon price used to convert payments into traded reductions Currency per unit of emissions Emission trading only

The exact units are determined by the configured model units. With the default units, emissions flows are expressed per year and costs are expressed in trillion 2010 US dollars per year.

docs.title: Checking emission-trading results
docs.text:
For every timestep with emission trading, the payments sum to zero across regions:

\[ \sum_r \href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}} = 0. \]

Because all payments are converted at the same global carbon price, the emission reduction trading balances also sum to zero. Therefore, trading changes the regional attribution of reductions and costs, but not their global totals. Small non-zero sums can occur in numerical results because of solver tolerances.

The regional emission allowances are calculated from the reductions attributed to a region:

\[ \href{./#var__regional_emission_allowances}{\text{regional emission allowances}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__attributed_emission_reductions}{\text{attributed emission reductions}_{t,r}}. \]

Without emission trading, regional_emission_allowances is simply equal to regional_emissions.

docs.title: Interaction with other modules
docs.text:
Emission trading is often used with an effort-sharing module. Effort sharing determines how allowances or costs should be distributed among regions, while emission trading connects that distribution to the physical reductions and costs in each region.

The financial transfer module is separate. Its transfers redistribute damage costs and do not change attributed_emission_reductions, regional_emission_allowances, or either emission-trading balance.

docs.title: Available options
docs.text:
No emission trade defaultWith emission trade

Usage: 

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["emissiontrade module"] = "notrade"
model = MIMOSA(params)

Without emission trading, both trading balances are always zero:

\[ \begin{align} \text{emission reduction trading balance}_{t,r} &= 0,\\ \text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r} &= 0. \end{align} \]

Therefore, the reductions attributed to a region are the physical reductions within that region, and mitigation_costs_abs is equal to domestic_mitigation_costs_abs (see Mitigation costs). The model does not create a separate attributed_emission_reductions result for this option.

Without trade, regional emission allowances are simply equal to regional emissions:

\[ \href{./#var__coacch::regional_emission_allowances}{\text{regional emission allowances}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__coacch::regional_emissions}{\text{regional emissions}_{t,r}}. \] Source code in mimosa/components/emissiontrade/notrade.py 
def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    Without emission trading, both trading balances are always zero:

    $$
    \begin{align}
    \text{emission reduction trading balance}_{t,r} &= 0,\\
    \text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r} &= 0.
    \end{align}
    $$

    Therefore, the reductions attributed to a region are the physical reductions within that region, and
    `mitigation_costs_abs` is equal to `domestic_mitigation_costs_abs` (see
    [Mitigation costs](mitigation.md#mitigation-costs)). The model does not create a separate
    `attributed_emission_reductions` result for this option.

    Without trade, regional emission allowances are simply equal to regional emissions:

    $$
    \href{./#var__coacch::regional_emission_allowances}{\text{regional emission allowances}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__coacch::regional_emissions}{\text{regional emissions}_{t,r}}.
    $$
    """
    constraints = []  # No constraints here

    m.emission_reduction_trading_balance = Param(
        m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("emissionsrate_unit"), initialize=0
    )
    m.mitigation_cost_trading_balance = Param(
        m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("currency_unit"), initialize=0
    )
    m.regional_emission_allowances = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("emissionsrate_unit"),
        doc="Regional emission allowances without trading, equal to the region's physical net CO2 emissions.",
    )

    constraints.append(
        # When there is no emission trading, emission allowances are simply equal to the emissions
        RegionalEquation(
            m.regional_emission_allowances, lambda m, t, r: m.regional_emissions[t, r]
        )
    )

    return constraints

Usage: 

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["emissiontrade module"] = "emissiontrade"
model = MIMOSA(params)

In MIMOSA, every region can physically reduce its own emissions. The domestic cost is determined by the area under the MAC (see Mitigation). Emission trading allows the reductions and mitigation costs attributed to a region to differ from the reductions and costs occurring within that region.

The associated financial flow is captured by \(\href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}}\). A positive balance increases the mitigation costs attributed to a region; a negative balance reduces them. For every timestep, the sum of these transfers should be zero:

\[ \sum_r \href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}} = 0 \]

A single global carbon price is used to convert the financial flow (mitigation_cost_trading_balance) into a flow of attributed emission reductions (emission_reduction_trading_balance):

\[ \href{./#var__emission_reduction_trading_balance}{\text{emission reduction trading balance}_{t,r}} = \frac{\href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#var__global_carbon_price}{\text{global carbon price}_{t}}}, \]

where the global carbon price is the population weighted average of the regional carbon prices:

\[ \href{./#var__global_carbon_price}{\text{global carbon price}_{t}} = \frac{\sum_r \href{./#var__carbon_price}{\text{carbon price}_{t,r}} \cdot \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}}}{\sum_r \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}}}. \]

The emission reductions attributed to a region are calculated as the physical reductions in that region plus its emission reduction trading balance:

\[ \href{./#var__attributed_emission_reductions}{\text{attributed emission reductions}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__regional_emission_reductions}{\text{regional emission reductions}_{t,r}} + \href{./#var__emission_reduction_trading_balance}{\text{emission reduction trading balance}_{t,r}}. \]

Regional emission allowances are the baseline emissions minus the reductions attributed to the region:

\[ \href{./#var__regional_emission_allowances}{\text{regional emission allowances}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__attributed_emission_reductions}{\text{attributed emission reductions}_{t,r}}. \] Source code in mimosa/components/emissiontrade/emissiontrade.py 
def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    In MIMOSA, every region can physically reduce its own emissions. The domestic cost is determined
    by the area under the MAC (see [Mitigation](mitigation.md#mitigation-costs)). Emission trading
    allows the reductions and mitigation costs attributed to a region to differ from the reductions
    and costs occurring within that region.

    The associated financial flow is captured by
    $\href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}}$. A positive balance increases the mitigation costs
    attributed to a region; a negative balance reduces them. For every timestep,
    the sum of these transfers should be zero:

    $$
    \sum_r \href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}} = 0
    $$

    A single global carbon price is used to convert the financial flow
    (`mitigation_cost_trading_balance`) into a flow of attributed emission reductions
    (`emission_reduction_trading_balance`):

    $$
    \href{./#var__emission_reduction_trading_balance}{\text{emission reduction trading balance}_{t,r}} = \frac{\href{./#var__mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#var__global_carbon_price}{\text{global carbon price}_{t}}},
    $$

    where the global carbon price is the population weighted average of the regional carbon prices:

    $$
    \href{./#var__global_carbon_price}{\text{global carbon price}_{t}} = \frac{\sum_r \href{./#var__carbon_price}{\text{carbon price}_{t,r}} \cdot \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}}}{\sum_r \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}}}.
    $$

    The emission reductions attributed to a region are calculated as the physical reductions in that region plus its
    emission reduction trading balance:

    $$
    \href{./#var__attributed_emission_reductions}{\text{attributed emission reductions}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__regional_emission_reductions}{\text{regional emission reductions}_{t,r}} + \href{./#var__emission_reduction_trading_balance}{\text{emission reduction trading balance}_{t,r}}.
    $$

    Regional emission allowances are the baseline emissions minus the reductions attributed to the region:

    $$
    \href{./#var__regional_emission_allowances}{\text{regional emission allowances}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__attributed_emission_reductions}{\text{attributed emission reductions}_{t,r}}.
    $$

    """
    constraints = []

    m.global_carbon_price = Var(
        m.t,
        doc="Population-weighted average of regional carbon prices, used to value emission trades.",
    )

    # Emissions are traded at the global carbon price
    constraints.extend(
        [
            # Constraint that sets the global carbon price to the average of the regional carbon prices:
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_carbon_price,
                lambda m, t: sum(
                    m.carbon_price[t, r] * m.population[t, r] for r in m.regions
                )
                / m.global_population[t],
            ),
        ]
    )

    ## Extra reporting variables:

    m.attributed_emission_reductions = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("emissionsrate_unit"),
        doc="Emission reductions attributed to a region after trading, equal to its physical emission reductions plus its emission-reduction trading balance.",
    )
    m.regional_emission_allowances = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("emissionsrate_unit"),
        doc="Regional emission allowances, equal to baseline emissions minus the emission reductions attributed to the region after trading.",
    )
    m.emission_reduction_trading_balance = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("emissionsrate_unit"),
        doc="Difference between attributed and physical emission reductions due to trading. Positive values increase the reductions attributed to the region; negative values decrease them.",
    )
    m.mitigation_cost_trading_balance = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        doc="Net payment for emission trading, added to domestic mitigation costs. Positive values are payments and negative values are revenues; the balances sum to zero across regions.",
    )
    constraints.extend(
        [
            GlobalConstraint(
                lambda m, t: sum(
                    m.mitigation_cost_trading_balance[t, r] for r in m.regions
                )
                == 0.0,
                "sum_mitigation_equals_sum_area_under_mac",
            ),
            # Convert the mitigation-cost trading balance into the emission-reduction trading balance
            RegionalEquation(
                m.emission_reduction_trading_balance,
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.mitigation_cost_trading_balance[t, r]
                    / soft_min(m.global_carbon_price[t])
                    if t > 0
                    else 0
                ),
            ),
            # Constraint: emission reductions attributed to the region after trading
            RegionalEquation(
                m.attributed_emission_reductions,
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.regional_emission_reductions[t, r]
                    + m.emission_reduction_trading_balance[t, r]
                    if t > 0
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
            ),
            # Constraint: regional emission allowances, equal to baseline minus attributed emission reductions
            RegionalEquation(
                m.regional_emission_allowances,
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.baseline_emissions[t, r] - m.attributed_emission_reductions[t, r]
                    if t > 0
                    else m.baseline_emissions[t, r]
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: Damage cost pool
docs.text:
Back to general structure

Besides emission trading, another mechanism to redistribute costs among regions is by allowing financial transfers to compensate for damage costs. In MIMOSA, two types can be chosen: either no financial transfers (default), or a global damage cost pool.

The financial transfer module can be chosen using the parameter financialtransfer module.

Unlike emission trading, financial transfers do not change the emission reductions attributed to a region or its regional emission allowances.

No transfers defaultGlobal damage cost pool

Usage: 

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["financialtransfer module"] = "notransfer"
model = MIMOSA(params)

Without financial transfers, this variable is always equal to zero:

\[ \text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r} = \text{financial transfer}_{t,r} = 0.0 \] Source code in mimosa/components/financialtransfer/notransfer.py 
def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    Without financial transfers, this variable is always equal to zero:

    $$
    \text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r} = \text{financial transfer}_{t,r} = 0.0
    $$
    """
    constraints = []

    # Since it is always zero, it is better to make it a Param instead of Var for numerical stability
    m.financial_transfer_abs = Param(
        m.t, m.regions, initialize=0, units=quant.unit("currency_unit")
    )
    m.financial_transfer = Param(
        m.t, m.regions, initialize=0, units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP")
    )

    return constraints

Usage: 

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["financialtransfer module"] = "globaldamagepool"
model = MIMOSA(params)

When allowing financial transfers for a global damage cost pool, a region can receive financial transfers up to its level of climate damages:

\[ \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r}} \geq - \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::damage_costs}{\text{damage costs}_{t,r}} \cdot \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross},t,r}} \]

The sum of financial transfers per time period should be zero, since it is a redistribution of costs:

\[ \sum_r \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r}} = 0 \]

Also, in the first year, no financial transfers are allowed:

\[ \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{0,r}} = 0. \]

financial_transfer_abs is expressed in currency units (dollars), while financial_transfer is expressed as a fraction of gross GDP:

\[ \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer}{\text{financial transfer}_{t,r}} = \frac{\href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross},t,r}}} \] Source code in mimosa/components/financialtransfer/globaldamagepool.py 
def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    When allowing financial transfers for a global damage cost pool, a region can
    receive financial transfers up to its level of climate damages:

    $$
    \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r}} \geq - \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::damage_costs}{\text{damage costs}_{t,r}} \cdot \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross},t,r}}
    $$

    The sum of financial transfers per time period should be zero, since it is a redistribution
    of costs:

    $$
    \sum_r \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r}} = 0
    $$

    Also, in the first year, no financial transfers are allowed:

    $$ \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{0,r}} = 0. $$

    `financial_transfer_abs` is expressed in currency units (dollars), while
    `financial_transfer` is expressed as a fraction of gross GDP:

    $$
    \href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer}{\text{financial transfer}_{t,r}} = \frac{\href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::financial_transfer_abs}{\text{financial transfer abs}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#var__financialtransfer_globaldamagepool::GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross},t,r}}}
    $$


    """
    constraints = []

    # Note: positive financial transfer means paying money, negative means receiving
    m.financial_transfer_abs = Var(
        m.t, m.regions, initialize=0, units=quant.unit("currency_unit")
    )
    m.financial_transfer = Var(
        m.t, m.regions, initialize=0, units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP")
    )

    constraints.extend(
        [
            GlobalConstraint(
                lambda m, t: (
                    sum(m.financial_transfer_abs[t, r] for r in m.regions) == 0.0
                    if t > 0
                    else Constraint.Skip
                ),
                "zero_sum_of_yearly_financial_transfer",
            ),
            RegionalInitConstraint(
                lambda m, r: m.financial_transfer_abs[0, r] == 0.0,
                "no_transfer_in_first_year",
            ),
            RegionalConstraint(
                lambda m, t, r: m.financial_transfer_abs[t, r]
                >= -m.damage_costs[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                "received_financial_transfer_max_own_damages",
            ),
            RegionalConstraint(
                lambda m, t, r: m.financial_transfer[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r]
                == m.financial_transfer_abs[t, r],
                "financial_transfer_rel_to_gdp",
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
Back to general structure

Marginal Abatement Costs (MAC) and mitigation costs Technological learning

In MIMOSA, the baseline emissions can be reduced by implementing a carbon price. This increases the price of carbon-intensive technologies relative to cleaner alternatives, which in turn leads to a reduction in emissions.

In MIMOSA, there are two ways in which the price of mitigation policy can be reduced over time: through learning by doing and learning over time. The learning factor is the product of these two factors.

Source code in mimosa/components/mitigation.py 
def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    """

    === ":material-chart-bell-curve-cumulative: Marginal Abatement Costs (MAC) and mitigation costs"

        :::mimosa.components.mitigation._get_mac_constraints

    === ":material-solar-power-variant-outline: Technological learning"

        :::mimosa.components.mitigation._get_learning_constraints

    """
    constraints = _get_mac_constraints(m, inputs) + _get_learning_constraints(m, inputs)

    return constraints

docs.title: Marginal Abatement Cost curve
docs.text: The carbon price required to reach a certain level of emission reduction is quantified by a Marginal Abatement Cost curve (MAC curve) and gives instantaneous reductions (emission reductions in a given year) relative to the baseline emissions. First, a global MAC curve is defined, which is then scaled for every region to give the regional MAC curve.

docs.title: Global MAC curve
docs.text:
The global MAC curve is defined as function of the relative mitigation \(a\) (percentage reduction of emissions compared to baseline emissions) and a time-dependent learning factor:

\[ \text{MAC}_t(a) = \left( \href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} \cdot a^{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}}\right) \cdot \href{./#var__learning_factor}{\text{learning factor}_t}. \]

The parameters \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma}\) (MAC_gamma) and \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}\) (MAC_beta) are calibrated using the IPCC AR6 WG3 report. The learning factor depends on learning by doing and learning over time (see the tab "Technological learning").

Calibrating the MAC using the IPCC AR6 WG3 report

docs.title: Step 1: calibration data source: IPCC AR6
docs.text:
Specifically, Figure 3.34c from the WGIII full report has been used to calibrate the MAC, as it gives discounted consumption losses from mitigation as function of cumulative CO2 emissions. However, for this use, the figure has been slightly recreated as function of cumulative CO2 emsisions from 2020 to 2100, instead of cumulative CO2 emissions from 2020 to the year of net-zero, to give a more accurate representation of mitigation costs for scenarios that reach net zero. The resulting mitigation costs are:

All costs are calculated as the NPV of GDP losses (as compared to the corresponding baseline GDP path for each scenario) with a fixed social discount rate of 3%/year, as used in the original IPCC AR6 figure.

docs.title: Step 2: fitting a function to the data
docs.text:
The next step is to fit a function through the cloud of points. We assume that the MAC is a power function (of a certain power \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}\)). This means that the abatement costs, being the integral of the MAC (area under the MAC) follows a function of power \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1\). We obtain the best fit (highest r-squared) with a power of \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}=3\), so a cubic MAC. We then perform an Ordinary Least Square regression of the function \(a \cdot x^4\) (a power function of \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1=4\)) and obtain the best fit shown as solid black line in figure 1:

Source of underlying GDP losses: IPCC AR6 WG3 Figure 3.34

docs.title: Step 3: calibrating MIMOSA to the fitted function
docs.text:
The final step is to calibrate the MAC used in MIMOSA to the OLS fit. In MIMOSA, this means calibrating the parameter \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma}\). When using

\[\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} = 2601 \text{ \$/tCO}_2,\]

the MIMOSA costs align best with the OLS fit through the AR6 points (see the diamond points in the previous figure).

docs.title: Regional MAC curve
docs.text:
The regional MAC curve is obtained by scaling the global MAC curve by a regional scaling factor, and links the regional carbon price to the regional mitigation level \(\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}\):

\[ \begin{align} \href{./#var__carbon_price}{\text{carbon price}_{t,r}} &= \text{MAC}_{\text{regional},t,r}(\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}})\\ &= \href{./#param__regional.MAC.kappa_rel_abatement_0.75_2050}{\text{regional scaling factor}_{r}} \cdot \text{MAC}_t(\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}})\\ &= \href{./#param__regional.MAC.kappa_rel_abatement_0.75_2050}{\text{regional scaling factor}_{r}} \cdot \left( \href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} \cdot \href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}^{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}}\right) \cdot \href{./#var__learning_factor}{\text{learning factor}_t}. \end{align} \]

The initial carbon price at time \(t=0\) is set to zero:

\[ \href{./#var__carbon_price}{\text{carbon price}_{0,r}} = 0. \] Source code in mimosa/components/mitigation.py 
def MAC(a, m, t, r):
    factor = (
        m.learning_factor[t] * m.MAC_scaling_factor[r] * m.MAC_SSP_calibration_factor[t]
    )
    return factor * m.MAC_gamma * a**m.MAC_beta

The regional scaling factor transforms the global MAC into a regional MAC:

The values of this regional scaling factor are calibrated using SSP2 MAC curves from the TIMER model (the energy submodule of IMAGE). By comparing the carbon price per region required to reach 75% CO2 reduction in 2050 compared to baseline, relative to the world average, we obtain a scaling factor for the MAC. The links show this default calibration; alternatives can be selected with regional calibration factor.

docs.title: Mitigation costs
docs.text:
The mitigation costs are calculated as area under the MAC:

Since the MAC is expressed in terms of mitigation level, we still need to multiply by the baseline emissions to obtain absolute mitigation costs in currency units (dollars). The area under the MAC, also called the absolute domestic mitigation costs, is therefore calculated as:

\[ \begin{align} \href{./#var__domestic_mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{domestic mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} &= \left(\int_0^{\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}} \text{MAC}_{\text{regional},t,r}(a)\ da \right) \cdot \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t,r}}\\ &= \text{factor}_{t,r} \cdot \frac{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} \cdot \href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}^{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1}}{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1} \cdot \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t,r}} \end{align} \]

Finally, the absolute mitigation costs attributed to a region are equal to its absolute domestic mitigation costs plus the mitigation cost trading balance if emission trading is enabled:

\[ \href{./#var__mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__domestic_mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{domestic mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} + \href{./#var__emissiontrade::mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}}. \]

docs.title: Mitigation costs as a fraction of GDP and their minimum level
docs.text:
In model output, mitigation_costs_abs contains the absolute costs in currency units and mitigation_costs contains the same costs as a fraction of gross GDP:

\[ \href{./#var__mitigation_costs}{\text{mitigation costs}_{t,r}} = \frac{\href{./#var__mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#var__GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross}, t,r}}}. \]

When emission trading is allowed, some regions may even have negative mitigation costs. How negative this can become can be configured with the parameter rel_mitigation_costs_min_level.

\[ \href{./#var__mitigation_costs}{\text{mitigation costs}_{t,r}} \geq \href{./#param__economics.MAC.rel_mitigation_costs_min_level}{\text{mitigation costs min level}}. \]

By default, this parameter is 0, meaning that the mitigation costs can not become negative.

docs.title: Parameters defined in this module
docs.text:
• params["economics"]["MAC"]["gamma"]: Calibration level of the MAC (carbon price for 100% reduction). Type: quantity. Default: 2887 USD2010/tCO2. Unit: currency_unit/emissionsrate_unit.
  • params["economics"]["MAC"]["beta"]: Power factor of the MAC curve. Type: float. Default: 3. Min: 0.01. Max: 10.
  • MAC_scaling_factor
  • params["economics"]["MAC"]["rel_mitigation_costs_min_level"]: Minimum level of mitigation costs (rel to GDP). By default, this is 0: no negative attributed mitigation costs are allowed. For certain effort-sharing regimes, this value can become negative to allow certain (small) financial transfers.. Type: float. Default: 0. Min: -2. Max: 0.
Source code in mimosa/components/mitigation.py 
def _get_mac_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    In MIMOSA, the baseline emissions can be reduced by implementing a carbon price. This increases the price of
    carbon-intensive technologies relative to cleaner alternatives, which in turn leads to a reduction in emissions.

    ## Marginal Abatement Cost curve

    The carbon price required to reach a certain level of emission reduction is quantified by a Marginal Abatement
    Cost curve (MAC curve) and gives instantaneous reductions (emission reductions in a given year) relative to the
    baseline emissions. First, a global MAC curve is defined, which is then scaled for every region to give the regional
    MAC curve.

    ### Global MAC curve

    The global MAC curve is defined as function of the relative mitigation $a$ (percentage reduction of emissions compared
    to baseline emissions) and a time-dependent learning factor:

    $$
    \text{MAC}_t(a) = \left( \href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} \cdot a^{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}}\right) \cdot \href{./#var__learning_factor}{\text{learning factor}_t}.
    $$

    The parameters $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma}$ ([`MAC_gamma`](#param__economics.MAC.gamma)) and $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}$ ([`MAC_beta`](#param__economics.MAC.beta))
    are calibrated using the IPCC AR6 WG3 report. The learning factor depends on learning by doing and learning over time
    (see the tab "Technological learning").

    ??? info "Calibrating the MAC using the IPCC AR6 WG3 report"

        ### Step 1: calibration data source: IPCC AR6

        Specifically, Figure 3.34c from the WGIII full report has been used to calibrate the MAC,
        as it gives discounted consumption losses from mitigation as function of cumulative CO2 emissions.
        However, for this use, the figure has been slightly recreated as function of cumulative CO2 emsisions
        from 2020 to 2100, instead of cumulative CO2 emissions from 2020 to the year of net-zero, to give a more
        accurate representation of mitigation costs for scenarios that reach net zero. The resulting mitigation costs
        are:


        All costs are calculated as the NPV of GDP losses (as compared to the corresponding baseline GDP path for each
        scenario) with a fixed social discount rate of 3%/year, as used in the original IPCC AR6 figure.

        ### Step 2: fitting a function to the data

        The next step is to fit a function through the cloud of points. We assume that the MAC is a power function
        (of a certain power $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}$). This means that the abatement costs, being the integral of the MAC
        (area under the MAC) follows a function of power $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1$. We obtain the best fit (highest r-squared)
        with a power of $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}=3$, so a cubic MAC. We then perform an Ordinary Least Square regression of the function
        $a \cdot x^4$ (a power function of $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1=4$) and obtain the best fit shown as solid black line in figure 1:

        ![Mitigation costs as GDP loss in the AR6 database](../assets/fig/calibration_ar6_mitig_costs.jpg)

        Source of underlying GDP losses: [IPCC AR6 WG3 Figure 3.34](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-3/#figure-3-34)

        ### Step 3: calibrating MIMOSA to the fitted function

        The final step is to calibrate the MAC used in MIMOSA to the OLS fit. In MIMOSA, this means calibrating the
        parameter $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma}$. When using

        $$\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} = 2601 \text{ \$/tCO}_2,$$

        the MIMOSA costs align best with the OLS fit through the AR6 points (see the diamond points in the previous figure).


    ### Regional MAC curve

    The regional MAC curve is obtained by scaling the global MAC curve by a regional scaling factor, and links the
    regional carbon price to the regional mitigation level $\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}$:

    $$
    \begin{align}
    \href{./#var__carbon_price}{\text{carbon price}_{t,r}} &= \text{MAC}_{\text{regional},t,r}(\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}})\\
    &= \href{./#param__regional.MAC.kappa_rel_abatement_0.75_2050}{\text{regional scaling factor}_{r}} \cdot \text{MAC}_t(\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}})\\
    &= \href{./#param__regional.MAC.kappa_rel_abatement_0.75_2050}{\text{regional scaling factor}_{r}} \cdot \left( \href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} \cdot \href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}^{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}}\right) \cdot \href{./#var__learning_factor}{\text{learning factor}_t}.
    \end{align}
    $$

    The initial carbon price at time $t=0$ is set to zero:

    $$
    \href{./#var__carbon_price}{\text{carbon price}_{0,r}} = 0.
    $$

    :::mimosa.components.mitigation.MAC
    The regional scaling factor transforms the global MAC into a regional MAC:


    ``` plotly
    {"file_path": "./assets/plots/MAC_kappa_rel_abatement_0.75_2050.json"}
    ```

    The values of this [regional scaling factor](#param__regional.MAC.kappa_rel_abatement_0.75_2050) are calibrated using SSP2 MAC curves from the TIMER model (the energy
    submodule of IMAGE). By comparing the carbon price per region required to reach 75% CO<sub>2</sub> reduction in 2050 compared to baseline,
    relative to the world average, we obtain a scaling factor for the MAC. The links show this default calibration;
    alternatives can be selected with [regional calibration factor](#param__economics.MAC.regional%20calibration%20factor).


    <h3 id="mitigation-costs">Mitigation costs</h3>

    The mitigation costs are calculated as area under the MAC:

    ``` {.plotly .center_align_plotly}
    {"file_path": "./assets/plots/mac_explanation.json"}
    ```

    Since the MAC is expressed in terms of mitigation level, we still need to multiply by the baseline emissions to obtain
    absolute mitigation costs in currency units (dollars). The area under the MAC, also called the
    absolute domestic mitigation costs, is therefore calculated as:

    $$
    \begin{align}
    \href{./#var__domestic_mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{domestic mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} &= \left(\int_0^{\href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}} \text{MAC}_{\text{regional},t,r}(a)\ da \right) \cdot \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t,r}}\\
    &= \text{factor}_{t,r} \cdot \frac{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.gamma}{\gamma} \cdot \href{./#var__mitigation_level}{a_{t,r}}^{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1}}{\href{./#param__economics.MAC.beta}{\beta}+1} \cdot \href{./#var__baseline_emissions}{\text{baseline emissions}_{t,r}}
    \end{align}
    $$

    Finally, the absolute mitigation costs attributed to a region are equal to its absolute domestic
    mitigation costs plus the mitigation cost trading balance if
    [emission trading](emissiontrading.md) is enabled:

    $$
    \href{./#var__mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__domestic_mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{domestic mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} + \href{./#var__emissiontrade::mitigation_cost_trading_balance}{\text{mitigation cost trading balance}_{t,r}}.
    $$


    ### Mitigation costs as a fraction of GDP and their minimum level
    In model output, `mitigation_costs_abs` contains the absolute costs in currency units and
    `mitigation_costs` contains the same costs as a fraction of gross GDP:

    $$
    \href{./#var__mitigation_costs}{\text{mitigation costs}_{t,r}} = \frac{\href{./#var__mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#var__GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross}, t,r}}}.
    $$

    When emission trading is allowed, some regions may even have negative mitigation costs. How negative this can become can
    be configured with the parameter [`rel_mitigation_costs_min_level`](#param__economics.MAC.rel_mitigation_costs_min_level).

    $$
    \href{./#var__mitigation_costs}{\text{mitigation costs}_{t,r}} \geq \href{./#param__economics.MAC.rel_mitigation_costs_min_level}{\text{mitigation costs min level}}.
    $$

    By default, this parameter is 0, meaning that the mitigation costs can not become negative.




    ## Parameters defined in this module
    - params["economics"]["MAC"]["gamma"]: Calibration level of the MAC (carbon price for 100% reduction). Type: quantity. Default: 2887 USD2010/tCO2. Unit: currency_unit/emissionsrate_unit.
    - params["economics"]["MAC"]["beta"]: Power factor of the MAC curve. Type: float. Default: 3. Min: 0.01. Max: 10.
    - MAC_scaling_factor
    - params["economics"]["MAC"]["rel_mitigation_costs_min_level"]: Minimum level of mitigation costs (rel to GDP). By default, this is 0: no negative attributed mitigation costs are allowed. For certain effort-sharing regimes, this value can become negative to allow certain (small) financial transfers.. Type: float. Default: 0. Min: -2. Max: 0.

    """

    constraints = []

    # MAC: linking the carbon price to the mitigation level
    m.MAC_gamma = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.MAC.gamma"))
    m.MAC_beta = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.MAC.beta"))
    calibration = inputs.config_value("economics.MAC.regional calibration factor")
    m.MAC_scaling_factor = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional("MAC", calibration),
    )  # Regional scaling of the MAC
    ssp = inputs.config_value("SSP")
    m.MAC_SSP_calibration_factor = Param(
        m.t,
        initialize=inputs.time_config(f"economics.MAC.SSP_calibration_factor.{ssp}"),
        units=quant.unit("dimensionless"),
    )
    m.carbon_price = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        bounds=lambda m: (0, 2 * m.MAC_gamma),
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit/emissions_unit"),
        doc="Regional carbon price required to achieve the mitigation level on the marginal abatement cost curve, accounting for regional and SSP calibration and technological learning. Set to zero at the initial timestep.",
    )
    constraints.extend(
        [
            RegionalEquation(
                m.carbon_price,
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    MAC(m.mitigation_level[t, r], m, t, r) if t > 0 else 0
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    # Mitigation costs

    # Mitigation costs equal domestic costs plus the mitigation-cost trading balance
    m.mitigation_costs_abs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        initialize=0,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        doc="Regional mitigation costs in currency units, equal to domestic mitigation costs plus the mitigation-cost trading balance.",
    )
    m.domestic_mitigation_costs_abs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        initialize=0,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        doc="Cost of emission reductions physically carried out in a region, calculated as the area under its marginal abatement cost curve times baseline emissions.",
    )
    m.mitigation_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Mitigation costs attributed to a region, including any mitigation-cost trading balance, divided by its gross GDP.",
    )
    m.mitigation_costs_min_level = Param(
        initialize=inputs.config("economics.MAC.rel_mitigation_costs_min_level")
    )
    constraints.extend(
        [
            # Domestic mitigation costs: area under the MAC times baseline emissions,
            # so the costs of mitigation in a region without taking into account emission trading
            RegionalEquation(
                m.domestic_mitigation_costs_abs,
                lambda m, t, r: AC(m.mitigation_level[t, r], m, t, r)
                * m.baseline_emissions[t, r],
            ),
            # Attributed mitigation costs: domestic costs plus the trading balance
            RegionalEquation(
                m.mitigation_costs_abs,
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.domestic_mitigation_costs_abs[t, r]
                    + m.mitigation_cost_trading_balance[t, r]
                ),
            ),
            RegionalEquation(
                m.mitigation_costs,
                lambda m, t, r: m.mitigation_costs_abs[t, r] / m.GDP_gross[t, r],
            ),
            RegionalConstraint(
                lambda m, t, r: m.mitigation_costs[t, r]
                >= (m.mitigation_costs_min_level if t > 0 else 0.0),
                "rel_mitigation_costs_non_negative",
            ),
        ]
    )

    # Keep track of relative global costs
    m.global_mitigation_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Global mitigation costs as a fraction of global gross GDP, calculated from the sum of regional mitigation costs.",
    )
    constraints.extend(
        [
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_mitigation_costs,
                lambda m, t: (
                    sum(m.mitigation_costs_abs[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                    / m.global_GDP_gross[t]
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    # Calculate average global emission reduction per cost unit
    # and average cost per unit emission reduction

    m.global_emission_reduction_per_cost_unit = Var(
        m.t,
        units=quant.unit("emissionsrate_unit / currency_unit"),
        doc="Average global CO2 emission reduction per unit of mitigation spending, calculated as total regional emission reductions divided by total mitigation costs. Set to zero at the initial timestep.",
    )
    m.global_cost_per_emission_reduction_unit = Var(
        m.t,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit / emissionsrate_unit"),
        doc="Average global mitigation cost per unit of CO2 emission reduction, calculated as total mitigation costs divided by total regional emission reductions. Set to zero at the initial timestep.",
    )
    constraints.extend(
        [
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_cost_per_emission_reduction_unit,
                lambda m, t: (
                    sum(m.mitigation_costs_abs[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                    / soft_min(
                        sum(m.regional_emission_reductions[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                    )
                    if t > 0
                    else 0
                ),
            ),
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_emission_reduction_per_cost_unit,
                lambda m, t: (
                    sum(m.regional_emission_reductions[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                    / soft_min(sum(m.mitigation_costs_abs[t, r] for r in m.regions))
                    if t > 0
                    else 0
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: Learning by doing
docs.text:
Learning by doing (endogenous technological learning) is a process where the cost of a technology decreases as more of it is produced. Here, the more mitigation has been done in the previous time steps, the cheaper the marginal abatement costs (MAC) become.

The learning by doing factor is defined as:

\[ \href{./#var__LBD_factor}{\text{LBD factor}_t} = \left( \href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_scaling}{\xi} \cdot \text{cumulative mitigation}_t + 1 \right)^{\log_2(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_rate}{\rho})}, \]

with \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_rate}{\rho}\) (LBD_rate) the progress ratio (i.e., the reduction in costs for doubling cumulative mitigation capacity) representing empirical studies of endogenous technological learning (see https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fclim.2021.785577/full).

\(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_scaling}{\xi}\) (LBD_scaling) is a scaling factor to transform the units of cumulative mitigation in relative terms (compared to baseline emissions in \(t=0\)).

The cumulative mitigation is equal to:

\[ \text{cumulative mitigation}_t = \text{baseline cum. emissions}_t - \href{./#var__global_cumulative_emissions}{\text{cum. emissions}_t}. \]

docs.title: Learning over time
docs.text:
Learning over time (exogenous technological learning) is a process where the cost of technology descreases over time, even if no mitigation has been done yet. The learning over time factor is defined as:

\[ \href{./#var__LOT_factor}{\text{LOT factor}_t} = \frac{1}{(1 + \href{./#param__economics.MAC.LOT_rate}{\lambda})^t}, \]

with \(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LOT_rate}{\lambda}\) (LOT_rate) the learning rate. By default, the learning over time rate is zero, so no learning over time is assumed.

docs.title: Parameters defined in this module
docs.text:
• params["economics"]["MAC"]["LBD_rate"]: Learning by doing rate: reduction in marginal mitigation costs for doubling cumulative mitigation capacity. Empirical studies show values between 0.65 (high learning) and 0.95 (low learning). Type: float. Default: 0.82. Min: 0.1. Max: 1.
  • params["economics"]["MAC"]["LBD_scaling"]: Scaling factor for learning by doing to transform the units of cumulative mitigation in relative terms (compared to baseline emissions in t=0). Only used for calibration, and should not be used to change the amount of LBD (for this, use economics > MAC > LBD_rate). Type: quantity. Default: 40 GtCO2. Unit: emissions_unit.
  • params["economics"]["MAC"]["LOT_rate"]: Learning rate of exogenous learning (learning over time). By default, there is no exogenous learning assumed, as all the technological learning happens endogenously (learning by doing).. Type: float. Default: 0. Min: 0. Max: inf.
Source code in mimosa/components/mitigation.py 
def _get_learning_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""

    In MIMOSA, there are two ways in which the price of mitigation policy can be reduced over time:
    through learning by doing and learning over time. The learning factor is the product of these two factors.

    ## Learning by doing

    Learning by doing (endogenous technological learning) is a process where the cost of a technology decreases as more of it is produced. Here,
    the more mitigation has been done in the previous time steps, the cheaper the marginal abatement costs (MAC) become.

    The learning by doing factor is defined as:

    $$
    \href{./#var__LBD_factor}{\text{LBD factor}_t} = \left( \href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_scaling}{\xi} \cdot \text{cumulative mitigation}_t + 1 \right)^{\log_2(\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_rate}{\rho})},
    $$

    with $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_rate}{\rho}$ ([`LBD_rate`](#param__economics.MAC.LBD_rate)) the progress ratio (i.e., the reduction in
    costs for doubling cumulative mitigation capacity) representing empirical studies of endogenous technological
    learning (see <https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fclim.2021.785577/full>).

    $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LBD_scaling}{\xi}$ ([`LBD_scaling`](#param__economics.MAC.LBD_scaling)) is a scaling factor
    to transform the units of cumulative mitigation in relative terms (compared to baseline emissions in $t=0$).

    The cumulative mitigation is equal to:

    $$
    \text{cumulative mitigation}_t = \text{baseline cum. emissions}_t - \href{./#var__global_cumulative_emissions}{\text{cum. emissions}_t}.
    $$


    ## Learning over time

    Learning over time (exogenous technological learning) is a process where the cost of technology descreases over time,
    even if no mitigation has been done yet. The learning over time factor is defined as:

    $$
    \href{./#var__LOT_factor}{\text{LOT factor}_t} = \frac{1}{(1 + \href{./#param__economics.MAC.LOT_rate}{\lambda})^t},
    $$

    with $\href{./#param__economics.MAC.LOT_rate}{\lambda}$ ([`LOT_rate`](#param__economics.MAC.LOT_rate)) the learning rate. By default, the learning over time
    rate is zero, so no learning over time is assumed.

    ## Parameters defined in this module
    - params["economics"]["MAC"]["LBD_rate"]: Learning by doing rate: reduction in marginal mitigation costs for doubling cumulative mitigation capacity. Empirical studies show values between 0.65 (high learning) and 0.95 (low learning). Type: float. Default: 0.82. Min: 0.1. Max: 1.
    - params["economics"]["MAC"]["LBD_scaling"]: Scaling factor for learning by doing to transform the units of cumulative mitigation in relative terms (compared to baseline emissions in t=0). Only used for calibration, and should not be used to change the amount of LBD (for this, use economics > MAC > LBD_rate). Type: quantity. Default: 40 GtCO2. Unit: emissions_unit.
    - params["economics"]["MAC"]["LOT_rate"]: Learning rate of exogenous learning (learning over time). By default, there is no exogenous learning assumed, as all the technological learning happens endogenously (learning by doing).. Type: float. Default: 0. Min: 0. Max: inf.

    """
    constraints = []

    ### Technological learning

    # Learning by doing
    m.LBD_rate = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.MAC.LBD_rate"))
    m.log_LBD_rate = Param(initialize=log(m.LBD_rate) / log(2))
    m.LBD_scaling = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.MAC.LBD_scaling"))
    m.LBD_factor = Var(
        m.t,
        doc="Multiplier on marginal abatement costs from learning by doing, based on cumulative emissions avoided relative to the SSP baseline through the preceding timestep. Starts at one; lower values mean cheaper mitigation.",
    )  # , bounds=(0,1), initialize=1)
    constraints.append(
        GlobalEquation(
            m.LBD_factor,
            lambda m, t: (
                soft_min(
                    (
                        m.global_cumulative_baseline_emissions[t - 1]
                        - m.global_cumulative_emissions[
                            t - 1
                        ]  # Now changed to t-1, check
                    )
                    / m.LBD_scaling
                    + 1.0
                )
                ** m.log_LBD_rate
                if t > 0
                else 1.0
            ),
        )
    )

    # Learning over time and total learning factor
    m.LOT_rate = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.MAC.LOT_rate"))
    m.LOT_factor = Var(
        m.t,
        doc="Multiplier on marginal abatement costs from exogenous technological progress, independent of mitigation undertaken. Starts at one; a positive learning rate reduces it at each model timestep.",
    )
    m.learning_factor = Var(
        m.t,
        doc="Combined technological-learning multiplier on marginal abatement costs, calculated as the product of the learning-by-doing and learning-over-time factors. Lower values mean cheaper mitigation.",
    )
    constraints.extend(
        [
            GlobalEquation(
                m.LOT_factor,
                lambda m, t: (1 / (1 + m.LOT_rate) ** t),
            ),
            GlobalEquation(
                m.learning_factor,
                lambda m, t: (m.LBD_factor[t] * m.LOT_factor[t]),
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: Region definitions
docs.text:
By default, MIMOSA uses the 26 IMAGE regions. More information about this regional definition is available on the IMAGE website.

The model region definition is named by the regionstype setting, while regions contains the region codes included in a run. The configuration schema also recognises SSP5 and World definitions. Using a different definition requires matching time-dependent input data and, where necessary, a registered mapping for regional parameters. See Regional parameters for details.

The map and table below describe the default IMAGE26 regions. Hover over the map to see a region's name:

The full country to region mapping can be downloaded from:

IMAGE26 country-to-region mapping

The default IMAGE26 abbreviations correspond to the following regions:

# Region Region name 1 CAN Canada 2 USA USA 3 MEX Mexico 4 RCAM Central America 5 BRA Brazil 6 RSAM Rest of South America 7 NAF Northern Africa 8 WAF Western Africa 9 EAF Eastern Africa 10 SAF South Africa 11 WEU Western Europe 12 CEU Central Europe 13 TUR Turkey 14 UKR Ukraine region 15 STAN Central Asia 16 RUS Russia region 17 ME Middle East 18 INDIA India 19 KOR Korea region 20 CHN China region 21 SEAS Southeast Asia 22 INDO Indonesia region 23 JAP Japan 24 OCE Oceania 25 RSAS Rest of South Asia 26 RSAF Rest of Southern Africa

docs.title: Sea-level rise
docs.text:
Back to general structure

The sea-level-rise (SLR) component represents thermal expansion, glaciers, the Greenland ice sheet (GIS), the Antarctic ice sheet (AIS), and future changes in land-water storage (LWS). The formulation is deliberately small and deterministic so it can be evaluated both by the MIMOSA simulator and as part of the Pyomo optimisation model.

All component values are expressed as metres above the 1900 global mean sea-level reference. The values at the model start are linearly interpolated between zero in 1900 and the central 2025 estimates below. This makes the reference year explicit and prevents a run starting before 2025 from using 2025 sea-level values.

The component option projection selects a coherent low, central, or high deterministic response set. The sets use identical historical initial conditions, but different sensitivities, response times, and AIS fast-response assumptions. The default is central.

The projection can be selected before model construction with:

params["sealevelrise"]["projection"] = "high"
Reference years and initial values

These values are shared by all three projections. Initial sea-level contributions are relative to the reference year and specified at the historical calibration year. At other start years, the model scales the initial values as described above. The land-water-storage anomaly starts at zero.

Symbol Meaning Units Value \(y_{\mathrm{ref}}\) Sea-level reference year year 1900 \(y_{\mathrm{init}}\) Historical calibration year year 2025 \(\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,fast,init}}\) Initial fast thermal-expansion contribution m 0.045 \(\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,slow,init}}\) Initial slow thermal-expansion contribution m 0.025 \(\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GL,init}}\) Initial glacier contribution m 0.09 \(\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GIS,init}}\) Initial Greenland contribution m 0.045 \(\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS,init}}\) Initial Antarctic contribution m 0.025 \(T_{\mathrm{A,init}}\) Initial Antarctic ocean-temperature proxy °C above pre-industrial 0.3

In the equations below, \(t\) indexes model time steps, \(\Delta t\) is the elapsed time in years, and \(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}\) is global mean warming above pre-industrial at the preceding step. A starred SLR value is the long-term equilibrium contribution at a fixed temperature; the actual contribution can lag behind that equilibrium.

docs.title: Thermal expansion
docs.text:
Thermal expansion is represented by a fast and a slow response box. Each box relaxes towards a temperature-dependent equilibrium:

\[ \begin{aligned} \href{./#var__slr_thermal_fast}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,fast},t}} &=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_fast_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{fast}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}} \\ &\quad+\left(\href{./#var__slr_thermal_fast}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,fast},t-1}}- \href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_fast_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{fast}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}\right) e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_fast_timescale}{\tau_{\mathrm{fast}}}}. \end{aligned} \] \[ \begin{aligned} \href{./#var__slr_thermal_slow}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,slow},t}} &=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_slow_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{slow}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}} \\ &\quad+\left(\href{./#var__slr_thermal_slow}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,slow},t-1}}- \href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_slow_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{slow}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}\right) e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_slow_timescale}{\tau_{\mathrm{slow}}}}. \end{aligned} \]

The total thermal-expansion contribution is the sum of the fast and slow contributions:

\[ \href{./#var__slr_thermal}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal},t}}= \href{./#var__slr_thermal_fast}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,fast},t}}+ \href{./#var__slr_thermal_slow}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,slow},t}}. \]

The exact exponential update makes the response independent of the chosen numerical time step for a constant temperature forcing.

This two-timescale formulation is a reduced-form approximation chosen for MIMOSA, rather than a direct reproduction of an ocean model. The first-order relaxation form follows BRICK v0.2 (Wong et al., 2017, Sect. 3.2.4, Eqs. 9--10). Splitting it into fast and slow boxes represents the upper- and deep-ocean distinction in SURFER v2.0 (Martínez Montero et al., 2022, Sects. 2.3.1 and 2.4.3). MIMOSA's equilibrium sensitivities and response times are calibrated jointly against the AR6 thermal-expansion contributions in Table 9.9 of Fox-Kemper et al. (2021); they are not the coefficients from either BRICK or SURFER.

docs.title: Glaciers
docs.text:
The glacier contribution relaxes towards the capped equilibrium proposed by Martínez Montero et al. (2022):

\[ \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GL}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gsic_total_ice}{P_{\mathrm{GL}}} \tanh\left(\frac{\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}}{\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gsic_temp_sensitivity}{\zeta_{\mathrm{GL}}}}\right), \] \[ \href{./#var__slr_cumgsic}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GL},t}}=\text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GL}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})+ \left(\href{./#var__slr_cumgsic}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GL},t-1}}-\text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GL}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})\right) e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gsic_timescale}{\tau_{\mathrm{GL}}}}. \]

This replaces the previous formulation, in which all glaciers eventually melted under any sustained temperature above -1 degree C.

Coefficients Symbol Meaning Units Low Central (default) High \(\zeta_{\mathrm{GL}}\) Equilibrium temperature scale °C 2.4 2 1.6 \(\tau_{\mathrm{GL}}\) Glacier response time years 120 110 140

Symbol Meaning Units Value \(P_{\mathrm{GL}}\) Glacier sea-level potential m 0.32

docs.title: Greenland ice sheet
docs.text:
The Greenland ice sheet contributes to sea-level rise as it loses ice. MIMOSA uses a SIMPLE-style delayed equilibrium: the temperature at the preceding step sets a long-term equilibrium contribution, and the actual contribution approaches that target gradually.

The equilibrium curve uses the logistic function

\[ \sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \]

a smooth transition from 0 to 1. Here \(x\) is a dimensionless argument. The equilibrium SLR contribution is normalised to zero at zero warming and approaches the ice sheet's sea-level potential at high warming:

\[ \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_total_ice}{P_{\mathrm{GIS}}} \frac{\sigma((\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_threshold}{T_c})/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_transition_width}{w})-\sigma(-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_threshold}{T_c}/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_transition_width}{w})} {1-\sigma(-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_threshold}{T_c}/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_transition_width}{w})}, \]

The response time \(\tau_{\mathrm{GIS}}\), measured in years, determines how quickly Greenland approaches this equilibrium. It decreases with warming, so higher temperatures lead to a faster response:

\[ \tau_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_base_timescale}{\tau_0}e^{-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_timescale_sensitivity}{\gamma} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}}. \]

The actual Greenland SLR contribution is updated each time step as

\[ \begin{aligned} \href{./#var__slr_cumgis}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GIS},t}} &= \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}) \\ &\quad + \left(\href{./#var__slr_cumgis}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GIS},t-1}} - \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})\right) e^{-\Delta t/\tau_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})}. \end{aligned} \]

Thus, only part of the gap to equilibrium closes within a model time step. For example, with a constant temperature and response time, about 63% of that gap closes after one response time. The actual SLR contribution, rather than the equilibrium target, is added to total sea-level rise.

The following constants are shared by all three projections.

Symbol Meaning Units Value \(P_{\mathrm{GIS}}\) Greenland sea-level potential m 7.3

docs.title: Antarctic ice sheet
docs.text:
A single lagged Antarctic subsurface-ocean temperature proxy drives the AIS response. A smooth threshold term represents the possibility of faster ice loss at high warming while retaining differentiability for optimisation.

The function \(\sigma\) is the same logistic function defined in the Greenland section above.

\[ \href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t}}=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_ocean_temp_scaling}{\lambda_A} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}+ \left(\href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t-1}}-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_ocean_temp_scaling}{\lambda_A} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}\right)e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_ocean_temp_timescale}{\tau_A}}, \] \[ \href{./#var__slr_cumais}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS},t}}=\href{./#var__slr_cumais}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS},t-1}}+\Delta t \left[\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_background_rate}{r_0}+\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_temp_sensitivity}{r_1}\href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t}}+\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_fast_rate}{r_f}\sigma((\href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t}}-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_fast_threshold}{T_{crit}})/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_fast_transition_width}{w_A})\right] \left(1-\frac{\href{./#var__slr_cumais}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS},t-1}}}{\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_total_ice}{P_{\mathrm{AIS}}}}\right). \]

The scaling and delay between global surface warming and Antarctic subsurface-ocean warming are motivated by LARMIP-2 (Levermann et al., 2020, Sect. 2.2). The AIS rate equation itself is a deliberately simpler MIMOSA parameterisation, not a reproduction of LARMIP-2 or SURFER. Its smooth fast term is inspired by the threshold representation of uncertain rapid Antarctic disintegration in Wong et al. (2017). The ordinary background and temperature-response rates are calibrated against the AR6 AIS contributions in Table 9.9. The high parameter set is intended as a low-likelihood, high-impact sensitivity case and not as the upper endpoint of the AR6 likely range.

docs.title: Calibration against IPCC AR6
docs.text:
The process papers motivate the compact equation forms; they do not imply that every coefficient is transferred unchanged. The three coherent parameter sets are outcome-calibrated against AR6 WGI Table 9.9 and the warming-level assessment in Chapter 12. Consequently, increasing the glacier or ordinary AIS response remains consistent with the cited equation structure while bringing total SLR into the assessed AR6 ranges. The following benchmark prescribes a linear warming path from 1.27 degrees C in 2025 to the stated 2100 warming level. Values are metres relative to 1900:
