def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    The sea-level-rise (SLR) component represents thermal expansion, glaciers,
    the Greenland ice sheet (GIS), the Antarctic ice sheet (AIS), and future
    changes in land-water storage (LWS). The formulation is deliberately small
    and deterministic so it can be evaluated both by the MIMOSA simulator and
    as part of the Pyomo optimisation model.

    All component values are expressed as metres above the 1900 global mean
    sea-level reference. The values at the model start are linearly interpolated
    between zero in 1900 and the central 2025 estimates below. This makes the
    reference year explicit and prevents a run starting before 2025 from using
    2025 sea-level values.

    The component option `projection` selects a coherent `low`, `central`, or
    `high` deterministic response set. The sets use identical historical
    initial conditions, but different sensitivities, response times, and AIS
    fast-response assumptions. The default is `central`.

    The projection can be selected before model construction with:

    ```python
    params["sealevelrise"]["projection"] = "high"
    ```

    {{ slr_coefficients("initial") }}

    In the equations below, $t$ indexes model time steps, $\Delta t$ is the
    elapsed time in years, and $\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}$ is global
    mean warming above pre-industrial at the preceding step. A starred SLR
    value is the long-term equilibrium contribution at a fixed temperature;
    the actual contribution can lag behind that equilibrium.

    # Thermal expansion

    Thermal expansion is represented by a fast and a slow response box. Each
    box relaxes towards a temperature-dependent equilibrium:

    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    \href{./#var__slr_thermal_fast}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,fast},t}}
    &=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_fast_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{fast}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}} \\
    &\quad+\left(\href{./#var__slr_thermal_fast}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,fast},t-1}}-
    \href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_fast_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{fast}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}\right)
    e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_fast_timescale}{\tau_{\mathrm{fast}}}}.
    \end{aligned}
    $$

    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    \href{./#var__slr_thermal_slow}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,slow},t}}
    &=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_slow_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{slow}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}} \\
    &\quad+\left(\href{./#var__slr_thermal_slow}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,slow},t-1}}-
    \href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_slow_sensitivity}{\beta_{\mathrm{slow}}} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}\right)
    e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_thermal_slow_timescale}{\tau_{\mathrm{slow}}}}.
    \end{aligned}
    $$

    The total thermal-expansion contribution is the sum of the fast and slow
    contributions:

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_thermal}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal},t}}=
    \href{./#var__slr_thermal_fast}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,fast},t}}+
    \href{./#var__slr_thermal_slow}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal,slow},t}}.
    $$

    The exact exponential update makes the response independent of the chosen
    numerical time step for a constant temperature forcing.

    This two-timescale formulation is a reduced-form approximation chosen for
    MIMOSA, rather than a direct reproduction of an ocean model. The first-order
    relaxation form follows BRICK v0.2 (Wong et al., 2017, Sect. 3.2.4,
    Eqs. 9--10). Splitting it into fast and slow boxes represents the upper- and
    deep-ocean distinction in SURFER v2.0 (Martínez Montero et al., 2022,
    Sects. 2.3.1 and 2.4.3). MIMOSA's equilibrium sensitivities and response
    times are calibrated jointly against the AR6 thermal-expansion contributions
    in Table 9.9 of Fox-Kemper et al. (2021); they are not the coefficients from
    either BRICK or SURFER.

    {{ slr_coefficients("thermal") }}

    # Glaciers

    The glacier contribution relaxes towards the capped equilibrium proposed
    by Martínez Montero et al. (2022):

    $$
    \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GL}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gsic_total_ice}{P_{\mathrm{GL}}}
    \tanh\left(\frac{\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}}{\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gsic_temp_sensitivity}{\zeta_{\mathrm{GL}}}}\right),
    $$

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_cumgsic}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GL},t}}=\text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GL}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})+
    \left(\href{./#var__slr_cumgsic}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GL},t-1}}-\text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GL}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})\right)
    e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gsic_timescale}{\tau_{\mathrm{GL}}}}.
    $$

    This replaces the previous formulation, in which all glaciers eventually
    melted under any sustained temperature above -1 degree C.

    {{ slr_coefficients("glaciers") }}

    # Greenland ice sheet

    The Greenland ice sheet contributes to sea-level rise as it loses ice.
    MIMOSA uses a SIMPLE-style delayed equilibrium: the temperature at the
    preceding step sets a long-term equilibrium contribution, and the actual
    contribution approaches that target gradually.

    The equilibrium curve uses the logistic function

    $$
    \sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}},
    $$

    a smooth transition from 0 to 1. Here $x$ is a dimensionless argument.
    The equilibrium SLR contribution is normalised to zero at zero warming
    and approaches the ice sheet's sea-level potential at high warming:

    $$
    \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_total_ice}{P_{\mathrm{GIS}}}
    \frac{\sigma((\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_threshold}{T_c})/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_transition_width}{w})-\sigma(-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_threshold}{T_c}/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_transition_width}{w})}
         {1-\sigma(-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_threshold}{T_c}/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_transition_width}{w})},
    $$

    The response time $\tau_{\mathrm{GIS}}$, measured in years, determines
    how quickly Greenland approaches this equilibrium. It decreases with
    warming, so higher temperatures lead to a faster response:

    $$
    \tau_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_base_timescale}{\tau_0}e^{-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_gis_timescale_sensitivity}{\gamma} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}}.
    $$

    The actual Greenland SLR contribution is updated each time step as

    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    \href{./#var__slr_cumgis}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GIS},t}}
    &= \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}) \\
    &\quad + \left(\href{./#var__slr_cumgis}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GIS},t-1}}
    - \text{SLR}^*_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})\right)
    e^{-\Delta t/\tau_{\mathrm{GIS}}(\href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}})}.
    \end{aligned}
    $$

    Thus, only part of the gap to equilibrium closes within a model time step.
    For example, with a constant temperature and response time, about 63% of
    that gap closes after one response time. The actual SLR contribution,
    rather than the equilibrium target, is added to total sea-level rise.

    {{ slr_coefficients("greenland") }}

    # Antarctic ice sheet

    A single lagged Antarctic subsurface-ocean temperature proxy drives the AIS
    response. A smooth threshold term represents the possibility of faster ice
    loss at high warming while retaining differentiability for optimisation.

    The function $\sigma$ is the same logistic function defined in the
    Greenland section above.

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t}}=\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_ocean_temp_scaling}{\lambda_A} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}+
    \left(\href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t-1}}-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_ocean_temp_scaling}{\lambda_A} \href{./#var__temperature}{T_{t-1}}\right)e^{-\Delta t/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_ocean_temp_timescale}{\tau_A}},
    $$

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_cumais}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS},t}}=\href{./#var__slr_cumais}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS},t-1}}+\Delta t
    \left[\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_background_rate}{r_0}+\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_temp_sensitivity}{r_1}\href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t}}+\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_fast_rate}{r_f}\sigma((\href{./#var__slr_antarctic_ocean_temp}{T_{A,t}}-\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_fast_threshold}{T_{crit}})/\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_fast_transition_width}{w_A})\right]
    \left(1-\frac{\href{./#var__slr_cumais}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS},t-1}}}{\href{./#slrcoef__slr_ais_total_ice}{P_{\mathrm{AIS}}}}\right).
    $$

    The scaling and delay between global surface warming and Antarctic
    subsurface-ocean warming are motivated by LARMIP-2 (Levermann et al., 2020,
    Sect. 2.2). The AIS rate equation itself is a deliberately simpler MIMOSA
    parameterisation, not a reproduction of LARMIP-2 or SURFER. Its smooth fast
    term is inspired by the threshold representation of uncertain rapid
    Antarctic disintegration in Wong et al. (2017). The ordinary background and
    temperature-response rates are calibrated against the AR6 AIS contributions
    in Table 9.9. The high parameter set is intended as a low-likelihood,
    high-impact sensitivity case and not as the upper endpoint of the AR6 likely
    range.

    {{ slr_coefficients("antarctica") }}

    # Land-water storage

    AR6 projects an approximately scenario-independent land-water contribution
    of 0.03 m between 1995--2014 and 2100. Because the historical contribution
    is already implicit in MIMOSA's 2025 initial total, only its future anomaly
    is added explicitly:

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_cumlws}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{LWS},t}}=\href{./#var__slr_cumlws}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{LWS},t-1}}+\Delta t\,\href{./#slrcoef__slr_lws_rate}{r_{\mathrm{LWS}}},
    \qquad \href{./#slrcoef__slr_lws_rate}{r_{\mathrm{LWS}}}=0.0004\ \mathrm{m\,yr^{-1}}.
    $$

    {{ slr_coefficients("land_water") }}

    # Total sea-level rise

    $$
    \href{./#var__total_SLR}{\text{SLR}_t}=\href{./#var__slr_thermal}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{thermal},t}}+\href{./#var__slr_cumgsic}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GL},t}}
        +\href{./#var__slr_cumgis}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{GIS},t}}+\href{./#var__slr_cumais}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{AIS},t}}+\href{./#var__slr_cumlws}{\text{SLR}_{\mathrm{LWS},t}}.
    $$

    ## Calibration against IPCC AR6

    The process papers motivate the compact equation forms; they do not imply
    that every coefficient is transferred unchanged. The three coherent
    parameter sets are outcome-calibrated against AR6 WGI Table 9.9 and the
    warming-level assessment in Chapter 12. Consequently, increasing the
    glacier or ordinary AIS response remains consistent with the cited equation
    structure while bringing total SLR into the assessed AR6 ranges. The
    following benchmark prescribes a linear warming path from 1.27 degrees C in
    2025 to the stated 2100 warming level. Values are metres relative to 1900:

    <div class="tiny_table table_first_col_header" markdown>
    {{ read_csv("docs/assets/data/slr_ar6_benchmark.csv") }}
    </div>

    The MIMOSA columns in this table and the component table below are generated
    directly from the current component equations. After changing the SLR
    formulation or parameters, regenerate both tables from the repository root:

    ```shell
    python diagnostics/slr_ar6.py
    ```

    A model test compares the committed CSV files with a fresh calculation so
    that outdated documentation is detected automatically.

    AR6 Chapter 12 reports the warming-level values relative to 1995--2014.
    The table adds the assessed 0.158 m rise from 1900 to 1995--2014, following
    the AR6 Summary for Policymakers. The comparison is a calibration diagnostic,
    not a claim that a warming level uniquely determines SLR: the preceding
    temperature pathway and rate of warming also affect the lagged components.

    Under this diagnostic, the low set tracks the lower edge of the AR6 likely
    range and central remains within it. High exceeds the likely range at 3 and
    4 degrees C by design, representing rapid Antarctic loss. For transparency,
    the central 2100 component values at 2, 3, and 4 degrees C respectively are:

    <div class="tiny_table table_first_col_header" markdown>
    {{ read_csv("docs/assets/data/slr_ar6_components.csv") }}
    </div>

    References:

    - [Fox-Kemper et al. (2021), IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 9](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-9/).
    - [IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 12, climate impact-driver projections](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-12/).
    - [IPCC AR6 WGI Summary for Policymakers](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/summary-for-policymakers/).
    - [Bakker, Applegate and Keller (2016), SIMPLE](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2016.05.003).
    - [Martínez Montero et al. (2022), SURFER v2.0](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-15-8059-2022).
    - [Wong et al. (2017), BRICK v0.2](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-10-2741-2017).
    - [Levermann et al. (2020), LARMIP-2](https://doi.org/10.5194/esd-11-35-2020).
    - [Wong, Bakker and Keller (2017), Antarctic fast dynamics](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-017-2039-4).
    """

    projection = inputs.config_value("sealevelrise.projection")
    try:
        slr_params = SLR_PROJECTION_PARAMETER_SETS[projection]
    except KeyError as exc:
        valid = ", ".join(SLR_PROJECTION_PARAMETER_SETS)
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown SLR projection parameter set '{projection}'. "
            f"Expected one of: {valid}."
        ) from exc

    # A common reference year and rounded central component values at the
    # default model start. Their 0.23 m sum is consistent with the assessed
    # historical rise and recent component trends. Values are metres of global
    # mean SLR above the 1900 reference.
    m.slr_reference_year = Param(initialize=1900)
    m.slr_initial_year = Param(initialize=2025)

    # Thermal expansion: fast upper-ocean and slow deep-ocean response boxes.
    m.slr_thermal_fast = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Global mean sea-level rise from the fast thermal-expansion response of the upper ocean, relative to 1900.",
    )
    m.slr_thermal_slow = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Global mean sea-level rise from the slow thermal-expansion response of the deep ocean, relative to 1900.",
    )
    m.slr_thermal = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Total global mean sea-level rise from ocean thermal expansion, relative to 1900. Sum of the fast and slow contributions.",
    )
    m.slr_thermal_fast_init = Param(initialize=0.045)
    m.slr_thermal_slow_init = Param(initialize=0.025)
    m.slr_thermal_fast_sensitivity = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["thermal_fast_sensitivity"]
    )
    m.slr_thermal_slow_sensitivity = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["thermal_slow_sensitivity"]
    )
    m.slr_thermal_fast_timescale = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["thermal_fast_timescale"]
    )
    m.slr_thermal_slow_timescale = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["thermal_slow_timescale"]
    )

    # Glaciers. The 0.32 m potential follows the AR6 parametric extrapolation.
    m.slr_cumgsic = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Global mean sea-level rise from the loss of glaciers and ice caps outside the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, relative to 1900.",
    )
    m.slr_gsic_init = Param(initialize=0.090)
    m.slr_gsic_total_ice = Param(initialize=0.32)
    m.slr_gsic_temp_sensitivity = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["gsic_temp_sensitivity"]
    )
    m.slr_gsic_timescale = Param(initialize=slr_params["gsic_timescale"])

    # Greenland. The potential is the sea-level equivalent of the full ice
    # sheet; the remaining parameters govern equilibrium and response speed.
    m.slr_cumgis = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Global mean sea-level rise from Greenland ice-sheet loss, relative to 1900. Gradually approaches a temperature-dependent equilibrium contribution.",
    )
    m.slr_gis_init = Param(initialize=0.045)
    m.slr_gis_total_ice = Param(initialize=7.3)
    m.slr_gis_threshold = Param(initialize=slr_params["gis_threshold"])
    m.slr_gis_transition_width = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["gis_transition_width"]
    )
    m.slr_gis_base_timescale = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["gis_base_timescale"]
    )
    m.slr_gis_timescale_sensitivity = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["gis_timescale_sensitivity"]
    )

    # Antarctica. The proxy temperature is in degrees C above pre-industrial;
    # rates are metres of sea-level equivalent per year.
    m.slr_antarctic_ocean_temp = Var(
        m.t,
        units=quant.unit("degC_above_PI"),
        doc="Antarctic subsurface-ocean temperature proxy above pre-industrial levels. Responds with a delay to global warming and drives Antarctic ice-sheet loss.",
    )
    m.slr_ais_ocean_temp_init = Param(initialize=0.30)
    m.slr_ais_ocean_temp_scaling = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["ais_ocean_temp_scaling"]
    )
    m.slr_ais_ocean_temp_timescale = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["ais_ocean_temp_timescale"]
    )
    m.slr_cumais = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Global mean sea-level rise from Antarctic ice-sheet loss, relative to 1900. Includes background loss, an ocean-temperature response, and a possible faster response at high warming.",
    )
    m.slr_ais_init = Param(initialize=0.025)
    # Effective vulnerable Antarctic stock, rather than the full AIS potential.
    m.slr_ais_total_ice = Param(initialize=5.0)
    m.slr_ais_background_rate = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["ais_background_rate"]
    )
    m.slr_ais_temp_sensitivity = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["ais_temp_sensitivity"]
    )
    m.slr_ais_fast_rate = Param(initialize=slr_params["ais_fast_rate"])
    m.slr_ais_fast_threshold = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["ais_fast_threshold"]
    )
    m.slr_ais_fast_transition_width = Param(
        initialize=slr_params["ais_fast_transition_width"]
    )

    # Future land-water-storage anomaly. Its historical contribution is
    # implicit in the common 2025 initial total, avoiding double counting.
    m.slr_cumlws = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Additional global mean sea-level rise from changes in land-water storage after the model start. Starts at zero and increases at a constant annual rate; historical land-water contributions are already included in the initial total sea level.",
    )
    m.slr_lws_rate = Param(initialize=0.0004)

    m.total_SLR = Var(
        m.t,
        within=NonNegativeReals,
        units=quant.unit("m"),
        doc="Total global mean sea-level rise relative to 1900. Sum of thermal expansion, glacier and ice-sheet loss, and future changes in land-water storage.",
    )

    constraints = [
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_thermal_fast,
            lambda m, t: (
                slr_thermal_expansion(
                    m.slr_thermal_fast[t - 1],
                    m.temperature[t - 1],
                    m.slr_thermal_fast_sensitivity,
                    m.slr_thermal_fast_timescale,
                    m,
                    m.period_length[t],
                )
                if t > 0
                else slr_initial_value(m.slr_thermal_fast_init, m)
            ),
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_thermal_slow,
            lambda m, t: (
                slr_thermal_expansion(
                    m.slr_thermal_slow[t - 1],
                    m.temperature[t - 1],
                    m.slr_thermal_slow_sensitivity,
                    m.slr_thermal_slow_timescale,
                    m,
                    m.period_length[t],
                )
                if t > 0
                else slr_initial_value(m.slr_thermal_slow_init, m)
            ),
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_thermal,
            lambda m, t: m.slr_thermal_fast[t] + m.slr_thermal_slow[t],
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_cumgsic,
            lambda m, t: (
                slr_gsic(
                    m.slr_cumgsic[t - 1],
                    m.temperature[t - 1],
                    m,
                    m.period_length[t],
                )
                if t > 0
                else slr_initial_value(m.slr_gsic_init, m)
            ),
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_cumgis,
            lambda m, t: (
                slr_gis(
                    m.slr_cumgis[t - 1],
                    m.temperature[t - 1],
                    m,
                    m.period_length[t],
                )
                if t > 0
                else slr_initial_value(m.slr_gis_init, m)
            ),
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_antarctic_ocean_temp,
            lambda m, t: (
                slr_antarctic_ocean_temperature(
                    m.slr_antarctic_ocean_temp[t - 1],
                    m.temperature[t - 1],
                    m,
                    m.period_length[t],
                )
                if t > 0
                else slr_initial_value(m.slr_ais_ocean_temp_init, m)
            ),
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_cumais,
            lambda m, t: (
                slr_ais(
                    m.slr_cumais[t - 1],
                    m.slr_antarctic_ocean_temp[t],
                    m,
                    m.period_length[t],
                )
                if t > 0
                else slr_initial_value(m.slr_ais_init, m)
            ),
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.slr_cumlws,
            lambda m, t: (
                m.slr_cumlws[t - 1]
                + m.period_length[t] * m.slr_lws_rate
                if t > 0
                else 0.0
            ),
        ),
        GlobalEquation(
            m.total_SLR,
            lambda m, t: (
                m.slr_thermal[t]
                + m.slr_cumgsic[t]
                + m.slr_cumgis[t]
                + m.slr_cumais[t]
                + m.slr_cumlws[t]
            ),
        ),
    ]

    return constraints

docs.text:
MIMOSA separates the calculation of yearly welfare1 from the final optimisation goal. There are three ways to calculate welfare: welfare-loss-minimising, cost-minimising, and a general inequality-aversion setting that connects the first two methods. The objective can then either maximise discounted welfare or minimise discounted global costs.

The welfare module can be chosen using the parameter welfare module.

In the equations below, \(\href{./#var__accreu_sectoral::non_market_damage_costs_abs}{D^{\mathrm{NM}}_{t,r}}\) denotes monetised non-market damages, such as mortality, in the same currency units as consumption. These damages reduce the consumption-equivalent input to welfare, while reported consumption \(\href{./#var__consumption}{C_{t,r}}\) remains physical consumption. The deduction is zero when non-market damages are not included.

Welfare-loss-minimising defaultCost-minimisingGeneral inequality aversion

Usage: 

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["welfare module"] = "welfare_loss_minimising"
model = MIMOSA(params)

Welfare-loss-minimising setting

In welfare-loss-minimising setting, the utility is first calculated regionally from the per capita consumption. These regional utilities are then summed up to get the global welfare. This means that costs are weighted differently in different regions, depending on the regional per capita consumption. As a consequence, this setting leads to differentiated carbon prices across regions: poorer regions typically will have lower carbon prices than richer regions.

Difference with cost-minimising setting

In the cost-minimising setting, the regional per capita consumption values are first added up to a global per capita consumption. The utility function is only then applied to this global per capita consumption to obtain global welfare.

Equations

First, calculate regional utility from consumption after deducting non-market damages, and population: $$ \href{./#var__coacch::utility}{U_{t,r}} = \text{utility}\left(\href{./#var__coacch::consumption}{C_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__accreu_sectoral::non_market_damage_costs_abs}{D_{t,r}^{NM}}, \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}\right) $$

Second, the global welfare is calculated as the sum of the regional utility values weighted by population: $$ \href{./#var__coacch::global_welfare}{W_t} = \sum_r \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}} \cdot \href{./#var__coacch::utility}{U_{t,r}} $$

Utility function

The utility function is a concave function of per-capita consumption, given by:

\[ \text{utility}(C, L) = \left( \left(\frac{C}{L}\right)^{1 - \href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}} - 1 \right) \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}}\]

Here \(C\) is the consumption-equivalent input supplied after deducting non-market damages, and \(L\) is population. \(\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}\) is the elasticity of marginal utility. A value of \(\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}\) close to 1 approaches a logarithmic utility function:

Source code in mimosa/components/welfare/utility_fct.py 
def calc_utility(consumption, population, elasmu):
    r"""
    The utility function is a concave function of per-capita consumption, given by:

    $$ \text{utility}(C, L) = \left( \left(\frac{C}{L}\right)^{1 - \href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}} - 1 \right) \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}}$$

    Here $C$ is the consumption-equivalent input supplied after deducting non-market damages,
    and $L$ is [population](#param__timeandregional.population).
    $\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}$ is the elasticity of marginal utility. A value of $\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}$ close to 1 approaches a logarithmic utility function:
    ``` plotly
    {"file_path": "./assets/plots/utility_fct.json"}
    ```

    """

    # Note that the `soft_min` function is used to avoid division by zero
    return (soft_min(consumption / population) ** (1 - elasmu) - 1) / (1 - elasmu)

def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""

    <h3>Welfare-loss-minimising setting</h3>

    In welfare-loss-minimising setting, the utility is first calculated regionally
    from the per capita consumption. These regional utilities are then summed up to
    get the global welfare. This means that costs are weighted differently in different
    regions, depending on the regional per capita consumption. As a consequence, this
    setting leads to differentiated carbon prices across regions: poorer regions typically
    will have lower carbon prices than richer regions.

    ???+ info "Difference with cost-minimising setting"
        In the cost-minimising setting, the regional per capita consumption values
        are first added up to a global per capita consumption. The utility function
        is only then applied to this global per capita consumption to obtain global welfare.

    <h3>Equations</h3>

    First, calculate regional utility from consumption after deducting non-market damages, and population:
    $$ \href{./#var__coacch::utility}{U_{t,r}} = \text{utility}\left(\href{./#var__coacch::consumption}{C_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__accreu_sectoral::non_market_damage_costs_abs}{D_{t,r}^{NM}}, \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}\right) $$

    Second, the global welfare is calculated as the sum of the regional utility values weighted by population:
    $$ \href{./#var__coacch::global_welfare}{W_t} = \sum_r \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}} \cdot \href{./#var__coacch::utility}{U_{t,r}} $$

    <h3>Utility function</h3>
    :::mimosa.components.welfare.utility_fct.calc_utility


    <h3>Parameters defined in this module</h3>
    - params["economics"]["elasmu"]: Elasticity of marginal utility. Type: float. Default: 1.001. Min: 0.1. Max: 10.

    """
    constraints = []

    # Parameters
    m.elasmu = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.elasmu"))

    m.utility = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        initialize=0.1,
        doc="Regional per-capita utility, calculated from consumption after deducting monetised non-market damages, using the elasticity of marginal utility.",
    )
    m.global_welfare = Var(
        m.t,
        doc="Undiscounted global welfare at each timestep, calculated as the sum of regional per-capita utilities weighted by population.",
    )

    constraints.extend(
        [
            RegionalEquation(
                m.utility,
                lambda m, t, r: calc_utility(
                    m.consumption[t, r] - m.non_market_damage_costs_abs[t, r],
                    m.population[t, r],
                    m.elasmu,
                ),
            ),
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_welfare,
                lambda m, t: sum(
                    m.population[t, r] * m.utility[t, r] for r in m.regions
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

Cost-minimising setting

In cost-minimising setting, the global per-capita consumption is first calculated before applying the utility function. This means that costs are weighted equally across regions, regardless of the regional per capita consumption. As a consequence, this setting leads to uniform carbon prices across regions. This is quantitatively similar to using Negishi weights.

Difference with welfare-loss-minimising setting

In the welfare-loss-minimising setting, the utility function is applied to the regional per capita consumption values, and the regional utilities are then summed up to get the global welfare. This means that costs (from mitigation or damages) have a larger weight in the final welfare in poorer regions than in richer regions.

Equations

First, aggregate consumption after deducting non-market damages, and population:

\[ \widehat{C}_{t} = \sum_r \left(\href{./#var__welfare_cost_minimising::consumption}{C_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__accreu_sectoral::non_market_damage_costs_abs}{D^{\mathrm{NM}}_{t,r}}\right), \] \[ \widehat{L}_{t} = \sum_r \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}. \]

These are used to calculate the global utility:

\[ \href{./#var__welfare_cost_minimising::global_welfare}{W_t} = \widehat{L}_t \cdot \text{utility}\left( \widehat{C}_{t}, \widehat{L}_{t} \right) \] Utility function

The utility function is a concave function of per-capita consumption, given by:

\[ \text{utility}(C, L) = \left( \left(\frac{C}{L}\right)^{1 - \href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}} - 1 \right) \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}}\]

Here \(C\) is the consumption-equivalent input supplied after deducting non-market damages, and \(L\) is population. \(\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}\) is the elasticity of marginal utility. A value of \(\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\text{elasmu}}\) close to 1 approaches a logarithmic utility function:

def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""

    <h3>Cost-minimising setting</h3>

    In cost-minimising setting, the global per-capita consumption is first calculated before
    applying the utility function. This means that costs are weighted equally across regions,
    regardless of the regional per capita consumption. As a consequence, this setting leads to
    uniform carbon prices across regions. This is quantitatively similar to using Negishi weights.

    ???+ info "Difference with welfare-loss-minimising setting"
        In the welfare-loss-minimising setting, the utility function is applied to the regional
        per capita consumption values, and the regional utilities are then summed up to get the
        global welfare. This means that costs (from mitigation or damages) have a larger weight in
        the final welfare in poorer regions than in richer regions.


    <h3>Equations</h3>

    First, aggregate consumption after deducting non-market damages, and population:

    $$ \widehat{C}_{t} = \sum_r \left(\href{./#var__welfare_cost_minimising::consumption}{C_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__accreu_sectoral::non_market_damage_costs_abs}{D^{\mathrm{NM}}_{t,r}}\right), $$

    $$ \widehat{L}_{t} = \sum_r \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}. $$

    These are used to calculate the global utility:

    $$ \href{./#var__welfare_cost_minimising::global_welfare}{W_t} = \widehat{L}_t \cdot \text{utility}\left( \widehat{C}_{t}, \widehat{L}_{t} \right) $$

    <h3>Utility function</h3>
    :::mimosa.components.welfare.utility_fct.calc_utility


    <h3>Parameters defined in this module</h3>
    - params["economics"]["elasmu"]: Elasticity of marginal utility. Type: float. Default: 1.001. Min: 0.1. Max: 10.

    """
    constraints = []

    # Parameters
    m.elasmu = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.elasmu"))

    m.utility = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        initialize=10,
        doc="Regional consumption per person after deducting monetised non-market damages, reported as the utility variable in the cost-minimising setting.",
    )
    m.global_welfare = Var(
        m.t,
        doc="Undiscounted global welfare, calculated by applying the utility function to global per-capita consumption after non-market damages and multiplying by global population.",
    )

    constraints.extend(
        [
            RegionalEquation(
                m.utility,
                lambda m, t, r: (
                    m.consumption[t, r] - m.non_market_damage_costs_abs[t, r]
                )
                / m.population[t, r],
            ),
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_welfare,
                lambda m, t: m.global_population[t]
                * calc_utility(
                    sum(
                        m.consumption[t, r] - m.non_market_damage_costs_abs[t, r]
                        for r in m.regions
                    ),
                    sum(m.population[t, r] for r in m.regions),
                    m.elasmu,
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

params["model structure"]["welfare module"] = "inequal_aversion_general"
model = MIMOSA(params)

General inequality aversion

This setting makes the weight given to inequality between regions explicit. Let \(\href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::consumption}{C_{t,r}}\) be regional consumption, \(\href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}\) population, \(\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}\) the inequality-aversion parameter (inequal_aversion), and \(\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}\) the elasticity of marginal utility (elasmu). MIMOSA first calculates:

\[ \href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::utility}{U_{t,r}} = \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}} \left(\frac{\href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::consumption}{C_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__accreu_sectoral::non_market_damage_costs_abs}{D^{\mathrm{NM}}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}}\right)^{1-\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}}. \]

The regional values are then aggregated into yearly welfare:

\[ \href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::global_welfare}{W_t} = \frac{L_t}{1-\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}} \left(\frac{\sum_r \href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::utility}{U_{t,r}}}{L_t}\right)^{ \frac{1-\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}}{1-\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}}}. \]

A higher \(\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}\) gives relatively more weight to consumption changes in poorer regions. Setting \(\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}=0\) gives the same policy weighting as the cost-minimising setting, while setting \(\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}=\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}\) gives the same policy weighting as the welfare-loss-minimising setting. The welfare levels can differ by terms that do not depend on the policy controls.

def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    <h3>General inequality aversion</h3>

    This setting makes the weight given to inequality between regions explicit. Let $\href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::consumption}{C_{t,r}}$
    be regional consumption, $\href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}$ population, $\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}$ the inequality-aversion parameter
    (`inequal_aversion`), and $\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}$ the elasticity of marginal utility (`elasmu`). MIMOSA first
    calculates:

    $$
    \href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::utility}{U_{t,r}} = \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}
    \left(\frac{\href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::consumption}{C_{t,r}} - \href{./#var__accreu_sectoral::non_market_damage_costs_abs}{D^{\mathrm{NM}}_{t,r}}}{\href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{L_{t,r}}}\right)^{1-\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}}.
    $$

    The regional values are then aggregated into yearly welfare:

    $$
    \href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::global_welfare}{W_t} = \frac{L_t}{1-\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}}
    \left(\frac{\sum_r \href{./#var__welfare_inequal_aversion_general::utility}{U_{t,r}}}{L_t}\right)^{
    \frac{1-\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}}{1-\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}}}.
    $$

    A higher $\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}$ gives relatively more weight to consumption changes in poorer regions.
    Setting $\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}=0$ gives the same policy weighting as the cost-minimising setting, while
    setting $\href{./#param__economics.inequal_aversion}{\eta}=\href{./#param__economics.elasmu}{\mu}$ gives the same policy weighting as the welfare-loss-minimising
    setting. The welfare levels can differ by terms that do not depend on the policy controls.

    <h3>Parameters defined in this module</h3>
    - params["economics"]["elasmu"]: Elasticity of marginal utility. Type: float. Default: 1.001. Min: 0.1. Max: 10.
    - param::inequal_aversion

    """
    constraints = []

    # Parameters
    m.elasmu = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.elasmu"))
    m.inequal_aversion = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.inequal_aversion"))

    m.utility = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        initialize=10,
        doc="Regional welfare contribution, equal to population times welfare-adjusted consumption per person raised to one minus inequality aversion. Welfare-adjusted consumption deducts monetised non-market damages.",
    )
    m.global_welfare = Var(
        m.t,
        doc="Undiscounted global welfare, calculated by aggregating regional welfare contributions with the configured inequality aversion and elasticity of marginal utility.",
    )

    constraints.extend(
        [
            RegionalEquation(
                m.utility,
                lambda m, t, r: calc_regional_utility(
                    m.consumption[t, r] - m.non_market_damage_costs_abs[t, r],
                    m.population[t, r],
                    m.inequal_aversion,
                ),
            ),
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_welfare,
                lambda m, t: sum(m.population[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                * calc_global_utility(
                    sum(m.utility[t, r] for r in m.regions),
                    m.global_population[t],
                    m.elasmu,
                    m.inequal_aversion,
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: Optimisation goal and discounting
docs.text:
The welfare module determines how regional consumption is aggregated into global_welfare. The separate objective module determines what MIMOSA optimises:

  • utility (default) maximises discounted global_welfare.
  • globalcosts minimises discounted mitigation and damage costs.

The objective can be selected in the model configuration:

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["objective module"] = "globalcosts"
model = MIMOSA(params)

With the utility objective, MIMOSA calculates:

\[ \href{./#var__NPV}{\text{NPV}_t} = \href{./#var__NPV}{\text{NPV}_{t-1}} + \Delta t \cdot e^{-\href{./#param__economics.PRTP}{\text{PRTP}}(\text{year}_t-\href{./#param__time.start}{\text{begin year}})} \cdot \href{./#var__global_welfare}{\text{yearly welfare}_t}, \]

This is a discrete approximation of the integral of discounted yearly welfare from the beginning year \(\href{./#param__time.start}{t_0}\) to the final year \(\href{./#param__time.end}{T}\):

\[ \href{./#var__NPV}{\text{NPV}}(\href{./#param__time.end}{T}) = \int_{\href{./#param__time.start}{t_0}}^{\href{./#param__time.end}{T}} e^{-\href{./#param__economics.PRTP}{\text{PRTP}}(t-\href{./#param__time.start}{t_0})} \cdot \href{./#var__global_welfare}{\text{yearly welfare}(t)}\, dt. \]

MIMOSA maximises the final value of NPV. With the global-cost objective, global_welfare is replaced by:

\[ \text{global costs}_t = \sum_r \left( \href{./#var__objective_globalcosts::mitigation_costs_abs}{\text{mitigation costs abs}_{t,r}} + \href{./#var__objective_globalcosts::damage_costs}{\text{damage costs}_{t,r}} \cdot \href{./#var__objective_globalcosts::GDP_gross}{\text{GDP gross}_{t,r}} \right), \]

and the final NPV is minimised. The welfare variables are still calculated in this case, but they do not determine the objective.

PRTP is the pure rate of time preference. A higher value gives less weight to outcomes further in the future. The factor \(\Delta t\) accounts for the number of years represented by each timestep.

The main result variables are:

Variable Meaning utility Regional utility or consumption measure, depending on the selected welfare module global_welfare Welfare aggregated across regions for one timestep NPV Discounted welfare under the utility objective, or discounted costs under the global-cost objective

  1. While the terms welfare and utility can be used interchangeably, we typically refer to utility as the regional utility, and welfare as the global population-weighted utility. ↩

docs.title: ACCREU damages and adaptation
docs.text:
Back to damage models

During the ACCREU project, new damage estimates were developed for riverine flooding, labour productivity, sea-level rise and mortality. Moreover, adaptation costs and effectiveness were estimated for all sectors (except mortality).

Usage:

Damages onlyDamages and adaptation 
params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["damage module"] = "ACCREU"
model = MIMOSA(params)

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["damage module"] = "ACCREU"
params["economics"]["damages"]["accreu"]["adaptation"] = "sectoral"
model = MIMOSA(params)

By default, only the damages are considered, without adaptation. Adaptation can be enabled with the parameter ACCREU adaptation set to sectoral. If adaptation is enabled, the regional adaptation costs for each sector become additional control variables (either optimised by the solver, or set by the user in simulation mode). The adaptation costs are then used to reduce the damages in sector \(i\) according to the adaptation level:

\[ \text{damages}_{i,t,r} = \text{gross damages}_{i,t,r} \cdot (1 - \text{adapt. level}_{i,t,r}), \]

The adaptation level is calculated as a function of absolute adaptation costs (in currency units) using a negative-exponential saturation (NES) curve:

\[ \text{NES}(\text{adapt. costs}_{i,t,r}; \cdot) = \text{max effectiveness}_{i,r} \cdot \left(1 - e^{-c_{i,r} \cdot \text{adapt. costs}_{i,t,r}}\right) \] Source code in mimosa/components/damages/accreu/utils.py 
def adaptation_effectiveness_fct(adapt_costs, max_effectiveness, cost_param):
    r"""
    The adaptation level is calculated as a function of absolute adaptation costs
    (in currency units) using a negative-exponential saturation (NES) curve:

    $$
    \text{NES}(\text{adapt. costs}_{i,t,r}; \cdot) = \text{max effectiveness}_{i,r} \cdot \left(1 - e^{-c_{i,r} \cdot \text{adapt. costs}_{i,t,r}}\right)
    $$
    """

    return max_effectiveness * (1 - exp(-cost_param * adapt_costs))

docs.text:
Riverine flooding Labour productivity Sea level rise Mortality

The impacts of riverine flooding are estimated using the GLOFRIS model. The gross damages are fitted with a quadratic function of temperature:

\[ \href{./#var__riverine_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} = (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_noadapt_ead_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_noadapt_ead_linear}{b_r} \cdot \href{./#var__temperature}{T_t} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_noadapt_ead_quadr}{c_r} \cdot \href{./#var__temperature}{T_t}^2) - (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_noadapt_ead_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_noadapt_ead_linear}{b_r} \cdot \href{./#param__temperature.initial}{T_0} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_noadapt_ead_quadr}{c_r} \cdot \href{./#param__temperature.initial}{T_0}^2). \]

The adaptation function is fitted with a negative-exponential saturation (NES) curve, like in all three sectors, using regional max. effectiveness and cost coefficient:

\[ \href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} = \text{NES}(\href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_costs_abs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{riverine},t,r}}; \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness}{\text{max eff.}_{\text{riverine},r}}, \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_adapt_eff_cost_param}{c_{\text{riverine},r}}) \]

Subsequently, the residual damages are calculated as:

\[ \href{./#var__riverine_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} = \href{./#var__riverine_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} \cdot (1 - \href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{riverine},t,r}}), \]

  • Global damages (without adaptation)

  • Global adaptation costs

Regional damage and adaptation functions Damages (without adaptation)Adaptation costs

Variables created in this module: riverine_damage_costs_gross: Gross damages from riverine flooding, without adaptation. Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. riverine_adaptation_costs_abs: Absolute adaptation costs for riverine flooding, in currency units. Used to calculate the adaptation level. Units: usd*trillion/yr; dimensions: t, regions. riverine_adaptation_costs: Adaptation costs for riverine flooding, as a fraction of GDP. Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. riverine_adaptation_level: Adaptation level for riverine flooding, as a fraction of gross damages. 0 means that no damages are avoided, while 1 means that all damages are avoided. Units: fraction_of_gross_damages; dimensions: t, regions. riverine_damage_costs: Residual damages from riverine flooding, after adaptation. If `noadaptation` is chosen, this variable represents the gross damages. Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. Source code in mimosa/components/damages/accreu/riverine_flooding.py 
def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs, adaptation_options: AdaptationOptions
):
    r"""

    The impacts of riverine flooding are estimated using the GLOFRIS model. The gross damages
    are fitted with a quadratic function of temperature:

    :::mimosa.components.damages.accreu.riverine_flooding.gross_dmg_fct_riverine
        options:
            show_source: false

    The adaptation function is fitted with a negative-exponential saturation (NES) curve, like in
    all three sectors, using regional [max. effectiveness](#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness) and [cost coefficient](#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_adapt_eff_cost_param):

    $$
    \href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{riverine},t,r}}
    = \text{NES}(\href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_costs_abs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{riverine},t,r}};
    \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness}{\text{max eff.}_{\text{riverine},r}},
    \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.riverine_adapt_eff_cost_param}{c_{\text{riverine},r}})
    $$

    Subsequently, the residual damages are calculated as:

    $$
    \href{./#var__riverine_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} = \href{./#var__riverine_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} \cdot (1 - \href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{riverine},t,r}}),
    $$

    <div class="grid cards" markdown>

    -   <h5 class="no-nav">Global damages (without adaptation)</h5>

        ---

        ``` plotly
        {"file_path": "./assets/plots/riverine_damages_global.json"}
        ```

    -   <h5 class="no-nav">Global adaptation costs</h5>

        ---

        ``` plotly
        {"file_path": "./assets/plots/riverine_adaptation_global.json"}
        ```
    </div>

    ??? regional-fct "Regional damage and adaptation functions"

        === "Damages (without adaptation)"

            ![Regional damage costs (without adaptation)](../../assets/fig/accreu/riverine_noadapt_ead.png)

        === "Adaptation costs"

            ![Regional damage costs (without adaptation)](../../assets/fig/accreu/riverine_adapt_eff.png)

    <div class="tiny_table table_scrollable extra_small" markdown>

    | Variables created in this module: |
    | --------------------------------- |
    | var::riverine_damage_costs_gross |
    | var::riverine_adaptation_costs_abs |
    | var::riverine_adaptation_costs |
    | var::riverine_adaptation_level |
    | var::riverine_damage_costs |

    </div>

    """

    constraints = []

    adaptation_type = adaptation_options.adaptation_type
    adaptation_calibration = adaptation_options.calibrations["riverine"]

    ## Gross damages:

    # m.riverine_damage_costs_gross_abs = Var(
    #     m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("currency_unit")
    # )

    m.riverine_damages_gross_constant = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "riverine_noadapt_ead_constant")
    )
    m.riverine_damages_gross_linear = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "riverine_noadapt_ead_linear")
    )
    m.riverine_damages_gross_quadr = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "riverine_noadapt_ead_quadr")
    )

    damage_cost_gross_var_name = (
        "riverine_damage_costs"
        if adaptation_type == "noadaptation"
        else "riverine_damage_costs_gross"
    )
    setattr(
        m,
        damage_cost_gross_var_name,
        Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Gross damages from riverine flooding, without adaptation.",
        ),
    )

    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(getattr(m, damage_cost_gross_var_name), gross_dmg_fct_riverine)
    )

    ## Adaptation:

    if adaptation_type == "sectoral":
        m.riverine_adaptation_costs_abs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
            bounds=lambda m, t, r: (0, 0.1 * m.baseline_GDP[t, r]),
            doc="Absolute adaptation costs for riverine flooding, in currency units. Used to calculate the adaptation level.",
        )
        m.riverine_adaptation_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Adaptation costs for riverine flooding, as a fraction of GDP.",
        )
        m.riverine_adaptation_level = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_gross_damages"),
            bounds=(0, 1),
            doc="Adaptation level for riverine flooding, as a fraction of gross damages. 0 means that no damages are avoided, while 1 means that all damages are avoided.",
        )
        m.riverine_damage_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Residual damages from riverine flooding, after adaptation. If `noadaptation` is chosen, this variable represents the gross damages.",
        )

        m.riverine_adaptation_max_effectiveness = Param(
            m.regions,
            initialize=inputs.regional(
                "ACCREU", "riverine_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness"
            ),
        )
        m.riverine_adaptation_cost_param = Param(
            m.regions,
            initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "riverine_adapt_eff_cost_param"),
        )
        constraints.append(
            get_delayed_adaptation_constraint("riverine_adaptation_costs")
        )
        constraints.extend(
            [
                # Adaptation effectiveness function
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.riverine_adaptation_level,
                    lambda m, t, r: adaptation_effectiveness_fct(
                        m.riverine_adaptation_costs_abs[t, r],
                        *effective_adaptation_curve(
                            m,
                            r,
                            m.riverine_adaptation_max_effectiveness[r],
                            m.riverine_adaptation_cost_param[r],
                            adaptation_calibration,
                        ),
                    ),
                ),
                # Adaptation costs as a fraction of GDP
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.riverine_adaptation_costs,
                    lambda m, t, r: m.riverine_adaptation_costs_abs[t, r]
                    / m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                ),
                # Residual damages after adaptation
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.riverine_damage_costs,
                    lambda m, t, r: m.riverine_damage_costs_gross[t, r]
                    * (1 - m.riverine_adaptation_level[t, r]),
                ),
            ]
        )

        if adaptation_options.uses_analytical_adaptation:
            constraints.append(
                # Calculate analytically the optimal level of adaptation
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.riverine_adaptation_costs_abs,
                    lambda m, t, r: optimal_adaptation_costs_fct(
                        m,
                        t,
                        m.riverine_damage_costs_gross[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                        *effective_adaptation_curve(
                            m,
                            r,
                            m.riverine_adaptation_max_effectiveness[r],
                            m.riverine_adaptation_cost_param[r],
                            adaptation_calibration,
                        ),
                    ),
                )
            )

    return constraints

The impact of climate change on labour productivity can be decomposed in two types: heat-related expected annual costs due to warming (e.g. hot regions get hotter, leading to reduced labour productivity), and cold-related expected annual benefits due to less cold days (especially relevant for currently cold regions).

The heat-related gross damage costs are fitted using a linear function of global temperature, shifted to 0 at the start year.

\[ \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} = (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_noadapt_ead_constant}{a_{r, \text{heat}}} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_noadapt_ead_linear}{b_{r, \text{heat}}} \cdot \href{./#var__temperature}{T_t}) - (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_noadapt_ead_constant}{a_{r, \text{heat}}} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_noadapt_ead_linear}{b_{r, \text{heat}}} \cdot \href{./#param__temperature.initial}{T_0}). \]

The cold-related benefits of climate change are also fitted using a linear function of global temperature, and shifted to 0 at the start year.

\[ \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs_benefits}{\text{benefits}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} = (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_benefit_cdd_constant}{a_{r, \text{cold}}} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_benefit_cdd_linear}{b_{r, \text{cold}}} \cdot \href{./#var__temperature}{T_t}) - (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_benefit_cdd_constant}{a_{r, \text{cold}}} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_benefit_cdd_linear}{b_{r, \text{cold}}} \cdot \href{./#param__temperature.initial}{T_0}). \]

The adaptation function, which only applies to heat-related gross damages, is fitted with a negative-exponential saturation (NES) curve, like in all three sectors, using regional max. effectiveness and cost coefficient:

\[ \href{./#var__labourprod_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} = \text{NES}(\href{./#var__labourprod_adaptation_costs_abs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}}; \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness}{\text{max eff.}_{\text{labourprod},r}}, \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.labourprod_adapt_eff_cost_param}{c_{\text{labourprod},r}}) \]

This leads to the residual, heat related damages:

\[ \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} = \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} \cdot (1 - \href{./#var__labourprod_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}}). \]

The final, net damages are calculated as the sum of the heat-related residual damages and the cold-related benefits:

\[ \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs_net}{\text{net damages}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} = \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} + \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs_benefits}{\text{benefits}_{\text{labourprod},t,r}} \]

  • Global damages (heat- and cold-related, without adapt.)

  • Global adaptation costs (only for heat-related damages)

Regional damage and adaptation functions Damages (without adaptation, heat-related)Benefits (from reduced cold)Adaptation costs

Variables created in this module: labourprod_damage_costs_gross: Gross damages from heat-related labour productivity loss (e.g. hot regions get hotter), without adaptation Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. labourprod_damage_costs_benefits: Benefits from reduced cold days for labour productivity (e.g. cold regions get less cold). No adaptation is applied to these benefits, as they are not related to heat stress. Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. labourprod_adaptation_costs_abs: Adaptation costs for labour productivity (absolute values) (applied only to heat-related damages, not cold-related benefits) Units: usd*trillion/yr; dimensions: t, regions. labourprod_adaptation_costs: Adaptation costs for labour productivity (as a fraction of GDP) (applied only to heat-related damages, not cold-related benefits) Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. labourprod_adaptation_level: Adaptation level for labour productivity (applied only to heat-related damages, not cold-related benefits) Units: fraction_of_gross_damages; dimensions: t, regions. labourprod_damage_costs: Residual damages for labour productivity after adaptation (heat-related component only) Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. labourprod_damage_costs_net: Sum of heat-related residual damages and cold-related benefits for labour productivity (net damages) Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. Source code in mimosa/components/damages/accreu/labour_productivity.py 
def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs, adaptation_options: AdaptationOptions

    r"""

    The impact of climate change on labour productivity can be decomposed in two types:
    heat-related expected annual costs due to warming (e.g. hot regions get hotter, leading
    to reduced labour productivity), and cold-related expected annual benefits due to less cold days

    | --------------------------------- |
    | var::labourprod_damage_costs_gross |
    | var::labourprod_damage_costs_benefits |
    | var::labourprod_adaptation_costs_abs |
    | var::labourprod_adaptation_costs |
    | var::labourprod_adaptation_level |
    | var::labourprod_damage_costs |
    | var::labourprod_damage_costs_net |

    </div>

    """

    constraints = []

    adaptation_type = adaptation_options.adaptation_type
    adaptation_calibration = adaptation_options.calibrations["labourprod"]

    ## Gross damages:

    damage_cost_gross_var_name = (
        "labourprod_damage_costs"
        if adaptation_type == "noadaptation"
        else "labourprod_damage_costs_gross"
    )

    setattr(
        m,
        damage_cost_gross_var_name,
        Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Gross damages from heat-related labour productivity loss (e.g. hot regions get hotter), without adaptation",
        ),
    )

    m.labourprod_damages_gross_constant = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "labourprod_noadapt_ead_constant"),
    )
    m.labourprod_damages_gross_linear = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "labourprod_noadapt_ead_linear")
    )

    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            getattr(m, damage_cost_gross_var_name), gross_dmg_fct_labourprod
        )
    )

    ## Benefits from less cooling demand due to higher temperatures (negative damages):

    m.labourprod_damage_costs_benefits = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Benefits from reduced cold days for labour productivity (e.g. cold regions get less cold). No adaptation is applied to these benefits, as they are not related to heat stress.",
    )

    m.labourprod_damages_benefits_constant = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "labourprod_benefit_cdd_constant"),
    )
    m.labourprod_damages_benefits_linear = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "labourprod_benefit_cdd_linear")
    )

    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            m.labourprod_damage_costs_benefits, benefits_dmg_fct_labourprod
        )
    )

    ## Adaptation (only for costs, doesn't apply to benefits):

    if adaptation_type == "sectoral":
        m.labourprod_adaptation_costs_abs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
            doc="Adaptation costs for labour productivity (absolute values) (applied only to heat-related damages, not cold-related benefits)",
            bounds=lambda m, t, r: (0, 0.1 * m.baseline_GDP[t, r]),
        )
        m.labourprod_adaptation_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Adaptation costs for labour productivity (as a fraction of GDP) (applied only to heat-related damages, not cold-related benefits)",
        )
        m.labourprod_adaptation_level = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_gross_damages"),
            bounds=(0, 1),
            doc="Adaptation level for labour productivity (applied only to heat-related damages, not cold-related benefits)",
        )
        m.labourprod_damage_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Residual damages for labour productivity after adaptation (heat-related component only)",
        )

        m.labourprod_adaptation_max_effectiveness = Param(
            m.regions,
            initialize=inputs.regional(
                "ACCREU", "labourprod_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness"
            ),
        )
        m.labourprod_adaptation_cost_param = Param(
            m.regions,
            initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "labourprod_adapt_eff_cost_param"),
        )
        constraints.append(
            get_delayed_adaptation_constraint("labourprod_adaptation_costs")
        )
        constraints.extend(
            [
                # Adaptation effectiveness function
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.labourprod_adaptation_level,
                    lambda m, t, r: adaptation_effectiveness_fct(
                        m.labourprod_adaptation_costs_abs[t, r],
                        *effective_adaptation_curve(
                            m,
                            r,
                            m.labourprod_adaptation_max_effectiveness[r],
                            m.labourprod_adaptation_cost_param[r],
                            adaptation_calibration,
                        ),
                    ),
                ),
                # Adaptation costs as a fraction of GDP
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.labourprod_adaptation_costs,
                    lambda m, t, r: m.labourprod_adaptation_costs_abs[t, r]
                    / m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                ),
                # Residual damages after adaptation
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.labourprod_damage_costs,
                    lambda m, t, r: m.labourprod_damage_costs_gross[t, r]
                    * (1 - m.labourprod_adaptation_level[t, r]),
                ),
            ]
        )

        if adaptation_options.uses_analytical_adaptation:
            constraints.append(
                # Calculate analytically the optimal level of adaptation
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.labourprod_adaptation_costs_abs,
                    lambda m, t, r: optimal_adaptation_costs_fct(
                        m,
                        t,
                        m.labourprod_damage_costs_gross[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                        *effective_adaptation_curve(
                            m,
                            r,
                            m.labourprod_adaptation_max_effectiveness[r],
                            m.labourprod_adaptation_cost_param[r],
                            adaptation_calibration,
                        ),
                    ),
                )
            )

    if adaptation_type != "combined":
        ## Net damages (costs + negative benefits):

        m.labourprod_damage_costs_net = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Sum of heat-related residual damages and cold-related benefits for labour productivity (net damages)",
        )

        constraints.append(
            RegionalEquation(
                m.labourprod_damage_costs_net,
                lambda m, t, r: m.labourprod_damage_costs[t, r]
                + m.labourprod_damage_costs_benefits[t, r],
            )
        )

    return constraints

The sea-level rise impacts are calculated using the DIVA model. Specifically, for this purpose, we compare the Constant Dike Height scenario (“no adaptation / CDH”) with three adaptation scenarios: Constant flood protection standards, Doubling flood protection standards, and Quadrupling flood protection standards. Importantly, we do not use the “optimal adaptation” scenario from DIVA, to avoid double optimisation in the IAMs.

The gross damages are fitted with a power function of global sea-level rise:

\[ \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} = \left(\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_noadapt_ead_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_noadapt_ead_prod}{b_r} \cdot \left(\href{./#var__total_SLR}{\text{SLR}_t}\right)^{\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_noadapt_ead_power}{c_r}}\right) - \left(\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_noadapt_ead_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_noadapt_ead_prod}{b_r} \cdot \left(\href{./#var__total_SLR}{\text{SLR}_0}\right)^{\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_noadapt_ead_power}{c_r}}\right) \]

The adaptation function is fitted with a negative-exponential saturation (NES) curve, like in all three sectors, using regional max. effectiveness and cost coefficient:

\[ \href{./#var__slr_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} = \text{NES}(\href{./#var__slr_adaptation_costs_abs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}; \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness}{\text{max eff.}_{\text{SLR},r}}, \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_adapt_eff_cost_param}{c_{\text{SLR},r}}) \]

Subsequently, the residual damages are calculated as:

\[ \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} = \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} \cdot (1 - \href{./#var__slr_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}), \]
