def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs, adaptation_options: AdaptationOptions
):
    r"""

    The sea-level rise impacts are calculated using the DIVA model. Specifically,
    for this purpose, we compare the Constant Dike Height scenario (“no adaptation / CDH”)
    with three adaptation scenarios: Constant flood protection standards, Doubling
    flood protection standards, and Quadrupling flood protection standards. Importantly,
    we do not use the “optimal adaptation” scenario from DIVA, to avoid double optimisation
    in the IAMs.

    The gross damages are fitted with a power function of global sea-level rise:

    :::mimosa.components.damages.accreu.sealevelrise.gross_dmg_fct_slr
        options:
            show_source: false

    The adaptation function is fitted with a negative-exponential saturation (NES) curve, like in
    all three sectors, using regional [max. effectiveness](#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness) and [cost coefficient](#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_adapt_eff_cost_param):

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}
    = \text{NES}(\href{./#var__slr_adaptation_costs_abs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{SLR},t,r}};
    \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness}{\text{max eff.}_{\text{SLR},r}},
    \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.slr_adapt_eff_cost_param}{c_{\text{SLR},r}})
    $$

    Subsequently, the residual damages are calculated as:

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} = \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs_gross}{\text{gross damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} \cdot (1 - \href{./#var__slr_adaptation_level}{\text{adapt. level}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}),
    $$

    <div class="grid cards" markdown>

    -   <h5 class="no-nav">Global damages (without adaptation)</h5>

        ---

        ``` plotly
        {"file_path": "./assets/plots/slr_damages_global.json"}
        ```

    -   <h5 class="no-nav">Global adaptation costs</h5>

        ---

        ``` plotly
        {"file_path": "./assets/plots/slr_adaptation_global.json"}
        ```
    </div>

    ??? regional-fct "Regional damage and adaptation functions"

        === "Damages (without adaptation)"

            ![Regional damage costs (without adaptation)](../../assets/fig/accreu/slr_noadapt_ead.png)

        === "Adaptation costs"

            ![Regional damage costs (without adaptation)](../../assets/fig/accreu/slr_adapt_eff.png)

    <div class="tiny_table table_scrollable extra_small" markdown>

    | Variables created in this module: |
    | --------------------------------- |
    | var::slr_damage_costs_gross |
    | var::slr_adaptation_costs_abs |
    | var::slr_adaptation_costs |
    | var::slr_adaptation_level |
    | var::slr_damage_costs |

    </div>
    """

    constraints = []
    adaptation_type = adaptation_options.adaptation_type
    adaptation_calibration = adaptation_options.calibrations["slr"]

    ## Gross damages:

    m.slr_damages_gross_constant = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "slr_noadapt_ead_constant")
    )
    m.slr_damages_gross_prod = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "slr_noadapt_ead_prod")
    )
    m.slr_damages_gross_power = Param(
        m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "slr_noadapt_ead_power")
    )

    damage_cost_gross_var_name = (
        "slr_damage_costs"
        if adaptation_type == "noadaptation"
        else "slr_damage_costs_gross"
    )
    setattr(
        m,
        damage_cost_gross_var_name,
        Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Gross damages from sea-level rise, without adaptation",
        ),
    )
    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            getattr(m, damage_cost_gross_var_name),
            gross_dmg_fct_slr,
        )
    )

    ## Adaptation:
    if adaptation_type != "noadaptation":
        m.slr_adaptation_costs_abs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
            bounds=lambda m, t, r: (0, 0.1 * m.baseline_GDP[t, r]),
            doc="Absolute adaptation costs for sea-level rise, in currency units. Used to calculate the adaptation level",
        )
        m.slr_adaptation_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Adaptation costs for sea-level rise, as a fraction of GDP.",
        )
        m.slr_adaptation_level = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_gross_damages"),
            bounds=(0, 1),
            doc="Adaptation level for sea-level rise, as a fraction of gross damages. 0 means that no damages are avoided, while 1 means that all damages are avoided.",
        )
        m.slr_damage_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Residual damages from sea-level rise, after adaptation. If `noadaptation` is chosen, this variable represents the gross damages.",
        )

        m.slr_adaptation_max_effectiveness = Param(
            m.regions,
            initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "slr_adapt_eff_max_effectiveness"),
        )
        m.slr_adaptation_cost_param = Param(
            m.regions,
            initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "slr_adapt_eff_cost_param"),
        )
        constraints.append(get_delayed_adaptation_constraint("slr_adaptation_costs"))
        constraints.extend(
            [
                # Adaptation effectiveness function
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.slr_adaptation_level,
                    lambda m, t, r: adaptation_effectiveness_fct(
                        m.slr_adaptation_costs_abs[t, r],
                        *effective_adaptation_curve(
                            m,
                            r,
                            m.slr_adaptation_max_effectiveness[r],
                            m.slr_adaptation_cost_param[r],
                            adaptation_calibration,
                        ),
                    ),
                ),
                # Adaptation costs as a fraction of GDP
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.slr_adaptation_costs,
                    lambda m, t, r: m.slr_adaptation_costs_abs[t, r]
                    / m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                ),
                # Residual damages after adaptation
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.slr_damage_costs,
                    lambda m, t, r: m.slr_damage_costs_gross[t, r]
                    * (1 - m.slr_adaptation_level[t, r]),
                ),
            ]
        )

        if adaptation_options.uses_analytical_adaptation:
            constraints.append(
                # Calculate analytically the optimal level of adaptation
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.slr_adaptation_costs_abs,
                    lambda m, t, r: optimal_adaptation_costs_fct(
                        m,
                        t,
                        m.slr_damage_costs_gross[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                        *effective_adaptation_curve(
                            m,
                            r,
                            m.slr_adaptation_max_effectiveness[r],
                            m.slr_adaptation_cost_param[r],
                            adaptation_calibration,
                        ),
                        scale=0.00001,
                    ),
                )
            )

    return constraints

docs.title: Physical impacts
docs.text:
The ACCREU damage representation includes temperature-related mortality impacts, though without accounting for explicit adaptation. Like labour productivity, there is a heat-related and cold-related component, varying strongly between regions. As global mean temperature increases, the heat-related mortality increases, while the cold-related mortality decreases.

The mortality forecasts are sourced from Bressler et al. (2021). The paper forecasts the change in future heat-related and cold-related mortality rates under RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0 and RCP 8.5 scenarios. It does so for the 2040-59 and 2080-99 periods. For this analysis, the estimates for these ranges are assigned to the years 2050 and 2090 respectively. In order to convert the forecasted change in the mortality rate into an estimate of excess mortality, the Bressler forecasts were combined with mortality rate forecasts from the World Bank (2025).

The heat-related mortality (as % of population) was fitted with a quadratic function. Given that they represent additional mortality relative to 2010, the fit was relative to temperature in 2010: 1.1 °C. To obtain a mortality value in absolute numbers, we multiply by total population:

\[ \href{./#var__mortality_heat_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{heat}, t, r}} = \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}} \cdot {\large(} (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r} \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_t} - 1.1)^2) - (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r} \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_0} - 1.1)^2) {\large)} \]

Cold-related mortality showed a linear relation with temperature, accounting for the fact that reductions in cold-related mortality don't become marginally larger when temperatures become very high. In fact, at some point we expect to see a plateau. However, the data doesn't show this behaviour for the assessed temperature range, where a linear fit throughout is the best fit:

\[ \href{./#var__mortality_cold_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{cold}, t, r}} = \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}} \cdot {\large(} (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r} \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_t} - 1.1)) - (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r} + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r} \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_0} - 1.1)) {\large)} \]

The total mortality is the sum of both:

\[ \href{./#var__mortality_net}{\text{mortality}_{\text{net},t,r}} = \href{./#var__mortality_heat_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{heat}, t, r}} + \href{./#var__mortality_cold_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{cold}, t, r}}. \]

  • Global mortality (heat- and cold-related, without adaptation)

Variables created in this module: mortality_heat_related: Extra heat-related mortality, in absolute numbers. Extra is compared to start year of the run (2025). Units: billion*people; dimensions: t, regions. mortality_cold_related: Reduced cold-related mortality, in absolute numbers, compared to start year of the run (2025). Units: billion*people; dimensions: t, regions. mortality_net: Sum of extra heat-related mortality and reduced cold-related mortality, in absolute numbers. Units: billion*people; dimensions: t, regions.

docs.title: Monetisation of mortality
docs.text:
If the MIMOSA parameter monetise mortality is set to true, the mortality values are converted to monetary value, which are then used by the welfare function:

params = load_params()
params["economics"]["damages"]["accreu"]["monetise_mortality"] = True # or False
model = MIMOSA(params)

Valuation of mortality in monetary units can be done using values of statistical life (VSL) or values of statistical life years (VSLY) multiplied by the expected life years lost. The main difference between these valuation methods is that the VSLY approach gives relatively lower values to mortality of people with a lower remaining life expectancy, while the VSL approach values mortality in all age classes equally.

Here, we follow the recommendation by the OECD to not adjust valuation according to the age of the population as this would imply that public policy and cost-benefit analysis outcomes could differ solely based on differences in the age of the populations studied. Moreover, little is known about the expected life years lost due to climate change impacts (Toulemon & Barbieri, 2008).

We therefore use the VSL approach for valuing the cost of mortality. The default MIMOSA value is the recommended estimates of the VSL from the OECD (2025). They provide a weighted world value of the VSL of 2.4 million dollars, which gives a \(\text{VSL}_{\text{rel}}\) of 117.59 times the GDP per capita.

The VSL in dollar terms is therefore:

\[ \href{./#var__mortality_vsl}{\text{VSL}_{\text{abs},t,r}} = \href{./#param__economics.damages.accreu.mortality_vsl_rel_gdp_cap}{\text{VSL}_{\text{rel}}} \cdot \frac{\href{./#var__GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross},t,r}}}{\href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}}} \]

The resulting mortality costs (in absolute terms) are given by:

\[ \begin{align} \href{./#var__mortality_damage_costs_abs}{\text{abs. damages}_{\text{mortality}, t, r}} &=\href{./#var__mortality_vsl}{\text{VSL}_{\text{abs},t,r}} \cdot (\href{./#var__mortality_heat_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{heat}, t, r}} + \href{./#var__mortality_cold_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{cold}, t, r}})\\ &= \href{./#var__non_market_damage_costs_abs}{\text{abs. damages}_{\text{non-market}, t,r}} \end{align} \]

Since these are the only non-market damages in the model, the non-market damages are equal to the mortality costs. These are not subtracted from GDP, but are removed in the welfare function. damages.

Variables created when mortality is monetised: mortality_vsl: Value of statistical life (VSL) in currency units, calculated as the relative VSL times GDP per capita Units: usd*trillion/yr; dimensions: t, regions. mortality_damage_costs_abs: Mortality damage costs in currency units. Since the extra heat-related deaths and reduced cold-related deaths are considered, this value can be positive or negative, depending on the region, time, and temperature. Units: usd*trillion/yr; dimensions: t, regions. mortality_damage_costs: Mortality damage costs expressed as % of GDP Units: fraction_of_GDP; dimensions: t, regions. Source code in mimosa/components/damages/accreu/mortality.py

    \begin{align}
        \href{./#var__mortality_damage_costs_abs}{\text{abs. damages}_{\text{mortality}, t, r}}
        &=\href{./#var__mortality_vsl}{\text{VSL}_{\text{abs},t,r}} \cdot (\href{./#var__mortality_heat_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{heat}, t, r}}
        + \href{./#var__mortality_cold_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{cold}, t, r}})\\
        &= \href{./#var__non_market_damage_costs_abs}{\text{abs. damages}_{\text{non-market}, t,r}}
    \end{align}
    $$

    Since these are the only non-market damages in the model, the non-market damages are equal to the
    mortality costs. These are not subtracted from GDP, but are removed in the [welfare function](../welfare.md).
    damages. 

    <div class="tiny_table table_scrollable extra_small" markdown>

    | Variables created when mortality is monetised: |
    | --------------------------------- |
    | var::mortality_vsl |
    | var::mortality_damage_costs_abs |
    | var::mortality_damage_costs |

    </div>

    """

    # Calculate the monetary damages from mortality, using the value of a statistical life (VSL)
    m.mortality_vsl_rel_gdp_per_cap = Param(
        initialize=inputs.config("economics.damages.accreu.mortality_vsl_rel_gdp_cap")
    )

    m.mortality_vsl = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        doc="Value of statistical life (VSL) in currency units, calculated as the relative VSL times GDP per capita",
    )
    m.mortality_damage_costs_abs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        bounds=lambda m, t, r: (
            -0.1 * m.baseline_GDP[t, r],
            0.5 * m.baseline_GDP[t, r],
        ),
        doc="Mortality damage costs in currency units. Since the extra heat-related deaths and reduced cold-related deaths are considered, this value can be positive or negative, depending on the region, time, and temperature.",
    )
    m.mortality_damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Mortality damage costs expressed as % of GDP",
    )
    constraints = [
        RegionalEquation(
            m.mortality_vsl,
            lambda m, t, r: m.mortality_vsl_rel_gdp_per_cap
            * m.GDP_gross[t, r]
            / m.population[t, r],
        ),
        RegionalEquation(
            m.mortality_damage_costs_abs,
            lambda m, t, r: m.mortality_vsl[t, r]
            * (m.mortality_cold_related[t, r] + m.mortality_heat_related[t, r]),
        ),
        RegionalEquation(
            m.mortality_damage_costs,
            lambda m, t, r: m.mortality_damage_costs_abs[t, r] / m.GDP_gross[t, r],
        ),
    ]

    return constraints

def get_constraints(m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs, monetise_mortality=False):
    r"""

    ### Physical impacts

    The ACCREU damage representation includes temperature-related mortality impacts, though
    without accounting for explicit adaptation. Like labour productivity, there is a heat-related
    and cold-related component, varying strongly between regions. As global mean temperature increases,
    the heat-related mortality increases, while the cold-related mortality decreases.

    The mortality forecasts are sourced from Bressler et al. (2021). The paper forecasts the change in
    future heat-related and cold-related mortality rates under RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0 and RCP 8.5 scenarios.
    It does so for the 2040-59 and 2080-99 periods. For this analysis, the estimates for these ranges are assigned
    to the years 2050 and 2090 respectively. In order to convert the forecasted change in the mortality rate
    into an estimate of excess mortality, the Bressler forecasts were combined with mortality rate forecasts
    from the World Bank (2025).

    The heat-related mortality (as % of population) was fitted with a quadratic function. Given that they represent
    additional mortality relative to 2010, the fit was relative to temperature in 2010: 1.1 °C. To obtain a mortality
    value in absolute numbers, we multiply by total population:

    $$
    \href{./#var__mortality_heat_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{heat}, t, r}}
    = \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}}
    \cdot {\large(}
        (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r}
        + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r}
        \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_t} - 1.1)^2)
        - (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r}
        + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.heat_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r}
        \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_0} - 1.1)^2)
    {\large)}
    $$

    Cold-related mortality showed a linear relation with temperature, accounting for the fact that reductions in
    cold-related mortality don't become marginally larger when temperatures become very high. In fact, at some point
    we expect to see a plateau. However, the data doesn't show this behaviour for the assessed temperature range, where
    a linear fit throughout is the best fit:

    $$
    \href{./#var__mortality_cold_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{cold}, t, r}}
    = \href{./#param__timeandregional.population}{\text{population}_{t,r}}
    \cdot {\large(}
        (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r}
        + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r}
        \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_t} - 1.1))
        - (\href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_constant}{a_r}
        + \href{./#param__regional.ACCREU.cold_related_mortality_perc_prod}{b_r}
        \cdot (\href{./#var__temperature}{T_0} - 1.1))
    {\large)}
    $$

    The total mortality is the sum of both:

    $$
    \href{./#var__mortality_net}{\text{mortality}_{\text{net},t,r}}
    = \href{./#var__mortality_heat_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{heat}, t, r}}
    + \href{./#var__mortality_cold_related}{\text{mortality}_{\text{cold}, t, r}}.
    $$


    <div class="grid cards" markdown>

    -   <h5 class="no-nav">Global mortality (heat- and cold-related, without adaptation)</h5>

        ---

        ``` plotly
        {"file_path": "./assets/plots/mortality_global.json"}
        ```
    </div>

    <div class="tiny_table table_scrollable extra_small" markdown>

    | Variables created in this module: |
    | --------------------------------- |
    | var::mortality_heat_related |
    | var::mortality_cold_related |
    | var::mortality_net |

    </div>

    ### Monetisation of mortality

    :::mimosa.components.damages.accreu.mortality._get_monetised_mortality_constraints

    """

    constraints = []

    ## Heat related mortality:
    m.mortality_heat_related = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("billion people"),
        doc="Extra heat-related mortality, in absolute numbers. Extra is compared to start year of the run (2025).",
    )

    m.mortality_heat_related_constant = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "heat_related_mortality_perc_constant"),
    )
    m.mortality_heat_related_prod = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "heat_related_mortality_perc_prod"),
    )

    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            m.mortality_heat_related,
            lambda m, t, r: m.population[t, r]
            * dmg_fct_power(
                m,
                t,
                m.mortality_heat_related_constant[r],
                m.mortality_heat_related_prod[r],
                2,
                xshift=1.1,
            ),
        )
    )

    ## Cold related mortality:
    m.mortality_cold_related = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("billion people"),
        doc="Reduced cold-related mortality, in absolute numbers, compared to start year of the run (2025).",
    )

    m.mortality_cold_related_constant = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "cold_related_mortality_perc_constant"),
    )
    m.mortality_cold_related_prod = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional("ACCREU", "cold_related_mortality_perc_prod"),
    )

    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            m.mortality_cold_related,
            lambda m, t, r: m.population[t, r]
            * dmg_fct_linear(
                m,
                t,
                m.mortality_cold_related_constant[r],
                m.mortality_cold_related_prod[r],
                xshift=1.1,
            ),
        )
    )

    ## Net mortality (heat + cold related):
    m.mortality_net = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("billion people"),
        doc="Sum of extra heat-related mortality and reduced cold-related mortality, in absolute numbers.",
    )
    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            m.mortality_net,
            lambda m, t, r: m.mortality_cold_related[t, r]
            + m.mortality_heat_related[t, r],
        )
    )

    if monetise_mortality:
        constraints.extend(_get_monetised_mortality_constraints(m, inputs))

    return constraints

docs.title: Total damages and adaptation
docs.text:
The total damage costs are the sum of the sectoral damages:

\[ \href{./#var__damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__riverine_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} + \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs_net}{\text{damages}_{\text{labour prod. (net)},t,r}} + \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}. \]

Similarly, if adaptation is enabled, the total adaptation costs are the sum of the sectoral adaptation costs:

\[ \href{./#var__adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} + \href{./#var__labourprod_adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{labour prod.},t,r}} + \href{./#var__slr_adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}. \]

As mentioned above, mortality is also included in this damage representation. However, since (the monetisation of) mortality is not represented as a direct cost to the economy, but rather a non-market impact, it is not included in the total damage costs. Instead, the monetised mortality costs are reported separately. If a user is interested in the sum of market and non-market damages, this is given by the variable market_and_non_market_damage_costs, calculated as:

\[ \href{./#var__market_and_non_market_damage_costs}{\text{market and non-market damages}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{t,r}} + \frac{\href{./#var__mortality_damage_costs_abs}{\text{abs. damages}_{\text{mortality},t,r}}}{\href{./#var__GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross},t,r}}}, \]

where \(\text{abs. damages}_{\text{mortality}}\) is the mortality damages in absolute terms (i.e. in currency units), and \(\text{GDP}_{\text{gross}}\) is the gross GDP, also in absolute terms (i.e. in currency units).

Variables created in this module: damage_costs: Total damages from all sectors (excluding non-market impacts like mortality), as a fraction of GDP. def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    The total damage costs are the sum of the sectoral damages:

    $$
    \href{./#var__damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__riverine_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} + \href{./#var__labourprod_damage_costs_net}{\text{damages}_{\text{labour prod. (net)},t,r}} + \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}.
    $$

    Similarly, if adaptation is enabled, the total adaptation costs are the sum of the sectoral adaptation costs:

    $$
    \href{./#var__adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__riverine_adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{riverine},t,r}} + \href{./#var__labourprod_adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{labour prod.},t,r}} + \href{./#var__slr_adaptation_costs}{\text{adapt. costs}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}.
    $$

    As mentioned above, mortality is also included in this damage representation. However, since (the monetisation of) mortality
    is not represented as a direct cost to the economy, but rather a non-market impact, it is not included in the total damage costs.
    Instead, the monetised mortality costs are reported separately. If a user is interested in the sum of market and non-market damages,
    this is given by the variable `market_and_non_market_damage_costs`, calculated as:

    $$
    \href{./#var__market_and_non_market_damage_costs}{\text{market and non-market damages}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{t,r}} + \frac{\href{./#var__mortality_damage_costs_abs}{\text{abs. damages}_{\text{mortality},t,r}}}{\href{./#var__GDP_gross}{\text{GDP}_{\text{gross},t,r}}},
    $$

    where $\text{abs. damages}_{\text{mortality}}$ is the mortality damages in absolute terms (i.e. in currency units),
    and $\text{GDP}_{\text{gross}}$ is the gross GDP, also in absolute terms (i.e. in currency units).

    <div class="tiny_table table_scrollable extra_small" markdown>

    | Variables created in this module: |
    | --------------------------------- |
    | var::damage_costs |
    | var::damage_costs_abs |
    | var::global_damage_costs |
    | var::adaptation_costs |
    | var::adaptation_costs_abs |
    | var::global_adaptation_costs |
    | var::non_market_damage_costs_abs |
    | var::market_and_non_market_damage_costs_abs |
    | var::market_and_non_market_damage_costs |

    </div>

    """

    constraints = []
    # In the config, the user can choose whether to use the separate adaptation module for ACCREU or not.
    # This is done using the parameter params["economics"]["damages"]["accreu"]["adaptation"] = "sectoral" or "combined"
    adaptation_options = get_adaptation_options(inputs)
    adaptation_type = adaptation_options.adaptation_type
    m.damage_scale_factor = Param(
        initialize=inputs.config("economics.damages.scale factor")
    )

    if adaptation_type != "noadaptation":
        m.adaptation_effectiveness_scale_factor = Param(
            initialize=inputs.config(
                "economics.damages.accreu.adaptation_effectiveness_scale_factor"
            )
        )

    # Get constraints for sea-level rise damages
    constraints.extend(sealevelrise.get_constraints(m, inputs, adaptation_options))

    # Get constraints for riverine flooding damages
    constraints.extend(riverine_flooding.get_constraints(m, inputs, adaptation_options))

    # Get constraints for labour productivity damages
    constraints.extend(
        labour_productivity.get_constraints(m, inputs, adaptation_options)
    )

    if adaptation_type == "combined":
        # Get constraints for combined adaptation costs, which combines labour productivity and riverine flooding adaptation costs
        # Only if the user has chosen to use the combined adaptation module for ACCREU
        constraints.extend(
            combined_nslr_adaptation.get_constraints(m, inputs, adaptation_options)
        )

    # Get constraints for mortality
    monetise_mortality = inputs.config_value(
        "economics.damages.accreu.monetise_mortality"
    )
    constraints.extend(
        mortality.get_constraints(m, inputs, monetise_mortality=monetise_mortality)
    )

    m.damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Total damages from all sectors (excluding non-market impacts like mortality), as a fraction of GDP.",
    )
    m.damage_costs_abs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        doc="Total damages from all sectors (excluding non-market impacts like mortality), in currency units.",
    )
    m.global_damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Global total damages from all sectors (excluding non-market impacts like mortality), as a fraction of global GDP.",
    )
    # Total damages are sum of non-SLR and SLR damages
    constraints.extend(
        [
            RegionalEquation(
                m.damage_costs,
                (
                    (
                        lambda m, t, r: m.combined_labprod_riv_damage_costs[t, r]
                        + m.slr_damage_costs[t, r]
                    )
                    if adaptation_type == "combined"
                    else (
                        lambda m, t, r: m.labourprod_damage_costs_net[t, r]
                        + m.riverine_damage_costs[t, r]
                        + m.slr_damage_costs[t, r]
                    )
                ),
            ),
            RegionalEquation(
                m.damage_costs_abs,
                lambda m, t, r: m.damage_costs[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r],
            ),
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_damage_costs,
                lambda m, t: (
                    sum(m.damage_costs_abs[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                    / m.global_GDP_gross[t]
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    if adaptation_type != "noadaptation":
        m.adaptation_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Total adaptation costs from all sectors, as a fraction of GDP.",
        )
        m.adaptation_costs_abs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
            doc="Total adaptation costs from all sectors, in currency units.",
        )
        m.global_adaptation_costs = Var(
            m.t,
            units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
            doc="Global total adaptation costs from all sectors, as a fraction of global GDP.",
        )
        m.delay_adaptation_year = Param(
            initialize=inputs.config(
                "economics.damages.accreu.delay_adaptation_until_year"
            )
        )
        constraints.extend(
            [
                # Adaptation costs:
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.adaptation_costs,
                    (
                        (
                            lambda m, t, r: m.combined_labprod_riv_adaptation_costs[
                                t, r
                            ]
                            + m.slr_adaptation_costs[t, r]
                        )
                        if adaptation_type == "combined"
                        else (
                            lambda m, t, r: m.labourprod_adaptation_costs[t, r]
                            + m.riverine_adaptation_costs[t, r]
                            + m.slr_adaptation_costs[t, r]
                        )
                    ),
                ),
                RegionalEquation(
                    m.adaptation_costs_abs,
                    lambda m, t, r: m.adaptation_costs[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r],
                ),
                GlobalEquation(
                    m.global_adaptation_costs,
                    lambda m, t: (
                        sum(m.adaptation_costs_abs[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                        / m.global_GDP_gross[t]
                    ),
                ),
            ]
        )
    else:
        m.adaptation_costs = Param(
            m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"), initialize=0.0
        )
        m.adaptation_costs_abs = Param(
            m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("currency_unit"), initialize=0.0
        )

    ## Non-market damages:
    if monetise_mortality:
        m.non_market_damage_costs_abs = Var(
            m.t,
            m.regions,
            units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
            doc="Total non-market damages (monetised mortality), in currency units.",
        )
        constraints.append(
            RegionalEquation(
                m.non_market_damage_costs_abs,
                lambda m, t, r: m.mortality_damage_costs_abs[t, r],
            )
        )
    else:
        m.non_market_damage_costs_abs = Param(
            m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("currency_unit"), initialize=0.0
        )
    m.market_and_non_market_damage_costs_abs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        doc="Total market and non-market damages, in currency units.",
    )
    m.market_and_non_market_damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Total market and non-market damages, as a fraction of GDP.",
    )

    constraints.extend(
        [
            RegionalEquation(
                m.market_and_non_market_damage_costs_abs,
                lambda m, t, r: m.damage_costs_abs[t, r]
                + m.non_market_damage_costs_abs[t, r],
            ),
            RegionalEquation(
                m.market_and_non_market_damage_costs,
                lambda m, t, r: m.market_and_non_market_damage_costs_abs[t, r]
                / m.GDP_gross[t, r],
            ),
        ]
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: COACCH damages
docs.text:
Back to damage models

Climate impacts in MIMOSA are calculated using the COACCH damage functions, developed in 2023 (see van der Wijst et al., 2023).

Usage:

params = load_params()
params["model structure"]["damage module"] = "COACCH" # This is the default damage module, so this line is optional.
model = MIMOSA(params)

The COACCH damage functions are split in two parts: temperature-dependent damages (non-SLR, as a function of global mean temperature above pre-industrial), and sea-level rise damages (SLR, as function of global mean sea-level rise in meters):

With combined damages, the temperature-dependent curve includes SLR impacts and the separate SLR damage term is zero.

\[ \href{./#var__damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__non_slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{non-SLR},t,r}} + \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} \]

docs.title: Temperature-dependent damages
docs.text:
The temperature-dependent damages are modeled as a quadratic damage function \(D(\cdot)\) of global mean temperature:

\[ D(x; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_1}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_2}) = \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_1} \cdot x + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_2} \cdot x^2. \]

To calculate the damages, three transformations have to be taken from the above quadratic equation:

  • The COACCH damage functions were created as function of temperature relative to 1986-2005, which is 0.6°C above pre-industrial. For this reason, the temperature is shifted by 0.6°C.
  • The damages are scaled by a factor \(a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r}\), which depends on the quantile \(\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q}\) of the damage function. This represents the uncertainty in the damage function. For median damages, this factor is \(\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_a%20%28q%3D0.5%29}{a_{0.5,r}} = 1\). The quantile can be set using the damage quantile parameter.
  • Since we assume that until 2020 the climate damages are already incorporated in the baseline GDP, we subtract the damages of the initial time period \(t=0\).

Combining these three transformations, the damages are calculated as:

\[ \href{./#var__non_slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{non-SLR},t,r}} = a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r} \cdot \big( D(\href{./#var__temperature}{\text{temperature}_t} - 0.6; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_{1,r}}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_{2,r}}) - D(\href{./#param__temperature.initial}{T_0} - 0.6; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_{1,r}}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_{2,r}}) \big). \]

The regional functional form and the coefficients above describe the separate non-SLR curve. Combined curves use their own coefficients, selected by quantile and adaptation.

All the damage coefficients are region-dependent (see Damage functions and coefficients).

def get_constraints_temperature_dependent(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    ## Temperature-dependent damages

    The temperature-dependent damages are modeled as a quadratic damage function $D(\cdot)$ of global mean temperature:

    $$
    D(x; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_1}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_2}) = \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_1} \cdot x + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_2} \cdot x^2.
    $$

    To calculate the damages, three transformations have to be taken from the above quadratic equation:

    * The COACCH damage functions were created as function of temperature relative to 1986-2005, which is 0.6°C above pre-industrial.
        For this reason, the temperature is shifted by 0.6°C.
    * The damages are scaled by a factor $a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r}$, which depends on the quantile $\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q}$ of the damage function. This represents the uncertainty
        in the damage function. For median damages, this factor is $\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_a%20%28q%3D0.5%29}{a_{0.5,r}} = 1$. The quantile can be set using the [damage quantile parameter](#param__economics.damages.quantile).
    * Since we assume that until 2020 the climate damages are already incorporated in the baseline GDP,
        we subtract the damages of the initial time period $t=0$.

    Combining these three transformations, the damages are calculated as:

    $$
    \href{./#var__non_slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{non-SLR},t,r}} = a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r} \cdot \big( D(\href{./#var__temperature}{\text{temperature}_t} - 0.6; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_{1,r}}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_{2,r}}) -  D(\href{./#param__temperature.initial}{T_0} - 0.6; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b1}{b_{1,r}}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_b2}{b_{2,r}}) \big).
    $$

    The [regional functional form](#param__regional.COACCH.NoSLR_form) and the coefficients above describe
    the separate non-SLR curve. Combined curves use their own coefficients, selected by quantile and adaptation.

    All the damage coefficients are region-dependent (see [Damage functions and coefficients](coacch.md#damage-functions-and-coefficients)).

    ### Temperature-dependent damages aggregated to the world, and comparison with the literature:

    ``` plotly
    {"file_path": "./assets/plots/coacch_literature_comparison.json"}
    ```

    """
    constraints = []
    combined = inputs.config_value(
        "economics.damages.coacch_combined_slr_nonslr_damages"
    )
    quantile = inputs.config_value("economics.damages.quantile")
    adapt_prefix = (
        "Ad"
        if inputs.config_value("economics.damages.coacch_slr_withadapt")
        else "NoAd"
    )

    # Damages not related to SLR (dependent on temperature)
    m.non_slr_damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Temperature-dependent regional damages as a fraction of gross GDP, relative to the model start. Includes sea-level-rise impacts when combined damage curves are selected.",
    )

    # Combined curves are quadratic and already incorporate the chosen quantile.
    m.damage_noslr_form = Param(
        m.regions,
        within=Any,
        initialize=(
            "Robust-Quadratic" if combined else inputs.regional("COACCH", "NoSLR_form")
        ),
    )  # String for functional form
    m.damage_noslr_b1 = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional(
            "COACCH",
            f"combined_b1_{adapt_prefix}-q{quantile}" if combined else "NoSLR_b1",
        ),
    )
    m.damage_noslr_b2 = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=inputs.regional(
            "COACCH",
            f"combined_b2_{adapt_prefix}-q{quantile}" if combined else "NoSLR_b2",
        ),
    )
    m.damage_noslr_b3 = Param(
        m.regions,
        within=Any,
        initialize=0 if combined else inputs.regional("COACCH", "NoSLR_b3"),
    )  # Can be empty
    # (b2 and b3 are only used for some functional forms)

    m.damage_noslr_a = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=(
            1 if combined else inputs.regional("COACCH", f"NoSLR_a (q={quantile})")
        ),
    )

    # Quadratic damage function for non-SLR damages. Factor `a` represents
    # the damage quantile
    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            m.non_slr_damage_costs,
            lambda m, t, r: (
                m.damage_scale_factor
                * damage_fct(m.temperature[t] - 0.6, m.T0 - 0.6, m, r, is_slr=False)
            ),
        )
    )

    return constraints

docs.title: Sea-level rise damages
docs.text:
In MIMOSA, sea-level rise damages are modelled separately from temperature dependent damages, as they occur on a different time scale: sea-level rise is a slow process with high inertia. Therefore, these damages are calculated as a function of global mean sea-level rise (SLR) in meters (calculated in the Sea-level rise component).

The SLR damages are calculated with the DIVA impact model (see Impact sectors used in the damage functions). These damages are available either with optimal adaptation (and include adaptation costs), or without adaptation. This can be chosen with the parameter coacch_slr_withadapt. By default, the optimal adaptation case is used.

Depending on the region, the SLR damages are modelled with different functional forms following from a best-fit regression. The SLR damages are either quadratic, linear, or logistic:

\[ D_{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_form}{\text{\{form\}}_r}}(\text{SLR}; \cdot) = \begin{cases} D_{\text{quadratic}}(\text{SLR}; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}) = \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1} \cdot \text{SLR} + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2} \cdot \text{SLR}^2\\[.2cm] D_{\text{linear}}(\text{SLR}; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}) = \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1} \cdot \text{SLR}\\[.2cm] D_{\text{logistic}}(\text{SLR}; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b3}{b_3}) = \frac{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}}{1 + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2} \cdot e^{-\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b3}{b_3} \cdot \text{SLR}}} - \frac{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}}{1 + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}} \end{cases} \]

The values of \(\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}\), \(\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}\), and \(\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b3}{b_3}\) are region-dependent and depend on whether adaptation is included or not. These are different values than the coefficients in the temperature-dependent damages. The functional forms depend on the regression of the underlying impact data (see Damage functions and coefficients) and are shown in the table below.

The coefficient links in the equations show the default, optimal-adaptation curve. Without adaptation, the corresponding regional inputs are the functional form, \(b_1\), \(b_2\), \(b_3\) and median scale factor.

Region SLR (with opt. adapt.) SLR (no adaptation) CAN Linear Quadratic USA Linear Quadratic MEX Linear Quadratic RCAM Linear Quadratic BRA Linear Quadratic RSAM Linear Quadratic NAF Linear Linear WAF Linear Linear EAF Linear Linear SAF Linear Quadratic WEU Logistic Linear CEU Logistic Quadratic TUR Linear Quadratic UKR Linear Quadratic STAN Linear Quadratic RUS Linear Quadratic ME Linear Quadratic INDIA Linear Linear KOR Linear Quadratic CHN Linear Quadratic SEAS Linear Linear INDO Linear Linear JAP Linear Linear OCE Linear Quadratic RSAS Logistic Quadratic RSAF Linear Linear

To calculate the SLR damage costs, two additional transformations have to be taken:

  • Similar to temperature-dependent damages, the SLR damages are scaled by a factor \(a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r}\), which depends on the quantile \(\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q}\) of the damage function. This represents the uncertainty in the damage function. For median damages, this factor is \(\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_a%20%28q%3D0.5%29}{a_{0.5,r}} = 1\). The quantile can be set using the damage quantile parameter.
  • Since we assume that until 2020 the climate damages are already incorporated in the baseline GDP, we subtract the damages of the initial time period \(t=0\).

The SLR damage costs therefore become:

\[ \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} = a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r} \cdot \big( D_{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_form}{\text{\{form\}}_r}}(\href{./#var__total_SLR}{\text{SLR}_t}; \cdot) - D_{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_form}{\text{\{form\}}_r}}(\href{./#var__total_SLR}{\text{SLR}_0}; \cdot) \big). \] Source code in mimosa/components/damages/coacch.py 
def get_constraints_slr(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""

    ## Sea-level rise damages

    In MIMOSA, sea-level rise damages are modelled separately from temperature dependent damages, as they occur
    on a different time scale: sea-level rise is a slow process with high inertia. Therefore, these damages are
    calculated as a function of global mean sea-level rise (SLR) in meters (calculated in the [Sea-level rise](../sealevelrise.md) component).

    The SLR damages are calculated with the DIVA impact model (see [Impact sectors used in the damage functions](coacch.md#impact-sectors-used-in-the-damage-functions)).
    These damages are available either with optimal adaptation (and include adaptation costs), or without adaptation. This can be
    chosen with the parameter [coacch_slr_withadapt](#param__economics.damages.coacch_slr_withadapt). By default, the optimal
    adaptation case is used.

    Depending on the region, the SLR damages are modelled with different functional forms following from a best-fit regression. The
    SLR damages are either quadratic, linear, or logistic:

    $$
    D_{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_form}{\text{\{form\}}_r}}(\text{SLR}; \cdot) = \begin{cases}
    D_{\text{quadratic}}(\text{SLR}; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}) = \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1} \cdot \text{SLR} + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2} \cdot \text{SLR}^2\\[.2cm]
    D_{\text{linear}}(\text{SLR}; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}) = \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1} \cdot \text{SLR}\\[.2cm]
    D_{\text{logistic}}(\text{SLR}; \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}, \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b3}{b_3}) = \frac{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}}{1 + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2} \cdot e^{-\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b3}{b_3} \cdot \text{SLR}}} - \frac{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}}{1 + \href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}}
    \end{cases}
    $$

    The values of $\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b1}{b_1}$, $\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b2}{b_2}$, and $\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_b3}{b_3}$ are region-dependent and depend on whether adaptation is included or not. These are different
    values than the coefficients in the temperature-dependent damages. The functional forms
    depend on the regression of the underlying impact data (see [Damage functions and coefficients](coacch.md#damage-functions-and-coefficients))
    and are shown in the table below.

    The coefficient links in the equations show the default, optimal-adaptation curve.
    Without adaptation, the corresponding regional inputs are the
    [functional form](#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-NoAd_form),
    [$b_1$](#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-NoAd_b1),
    [$b_2$](#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-NoAd_b2),
    [$b_3$](#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-NoAd_b3) and
    [median scale factor](#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-NoAd_a%20%28q%3D0.5%29).

    <div class="tiny_table table_first_col_header table_scrollable" markdown>
    {{ read_csv("docs/assets/data/coacch_slr_form.csv") }}
    </div>

    To calculate the SLR damage costs, two additional transformations have to be taken:

    * Similar to temperature-dependent damages, the SLR damages are scaled by a factor $a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r}$, which depends on the quantile $\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q}$ of the damage function.
        This represents the uncertainty in the damage function. For median damages, this factor is $\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_a%20%28q%3D0.5%29}{a_{0.5,r}} = 1$. The quantile can be set using the
        [damage quantile parameter](#param__economics.damages.quantile).
    * Since we assume that until 2020 the climate damages are already incorporated in the baseline GDP,
        we subtract the damages of the initial time period $t=0$.

    The SLR damage costs therefore become:

    $$
    \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}} = a_{\href{./#param__economics.damages.quantile}{q},r} \cdot \big( D_{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_form}{\text{\{form\}}_r}}(\href{./#var__total_SLR}{\text{SLR}_t}; \cdot) - D_{\href{./#param__regional.COACCH.SLR-Ad_form}{\text{\{form\}}_r}}(\href{./#var__total_SLR}{\text{SLR}_0}; \cdot) \big).
    $$

    """
    constraints = []
    combined = inputs.config_value(
        "economics.damages.coacch_combined_slr_nonslr_damages"
    )
    quantile = inputs.config_value("economics.damages.quantile")
    adapt_prefix = (
        "Ad"
        if inputs.config_value("economics.damages.coacch_slr_withadapt")
        else "NoAd"
    )

    # SLR damages
    m.slr_damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        bounds=(-0.5, 0.7),
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Regional sea-level-rise damages as a fraction of gross GDP, relative to initial sea level. Includes adaptation costs when optimal-adaptation curves are selected; zero when combined damage curves are used.",
    )

    # Combined curves already include SLR; keep the separate SLR parameters at zero.
    m.damage_slr_form = Param(
        m.regions,
        within=Any,
        initialize=(
            "Robust-Linear"
            if combined
            else inputs.regional("COACCH", f"SLR-{adapt_prefix}_form")
        ),
    )  # String for functional form
    m.damage_slr_b1 = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=(
            0 if combined else inputs.regional("COACCH", f"SLR-{adapt_prefix}_b1")
        ),
    )
    m.damage_slr_b2 = Param(
        m.regions,
        within=Any,
        initialize=(
            0 if combined else inputs.regional("COACCH", f"SLR-{adapt_prefix}_b2")
        ),
    )  # within=Any since it can be empty for some functional forms
    m.damage_slr_b3 = Param(
        m.regions,
        within=Any,
        initialize=(
            0 if combined else inputs.regional("COACCH", f"SLR-{adapt_prefix}_b3")
        ),
    )  # within=Any since it can be empty for some functional forms
    # (b2 and b3 are only used for some functional forms)

    m.damage_slr_a = Param(
        m.regions,
        initialize=(
            0
            if combined
            else inputs.regional("COACCH", f"SLR-{adapt_prefix}_a (q={quantile})")
        ),
    )

    # Linear damage function for SLR damages, including adaptation costs
    constraints.append(
        RegionalEquation(
            m.slr_damage_costs,
            lambda m, t, r: (
                m.damage_scale_factor
                * damage_fct(m.total_SLR[t], m.total_SLR[0], m, r, is_slr=True)
            ),
        )
    )

    return constraints

def get_constraints(
    m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs
) -> Sequence[GeneralConstraint]:
    r"""
    The COACCH damage functions are split in two parts: temperature-dependent damages (non-SLR, as a function
    of global mean temperature above pre-industrial), and sea-level rise damages (SLR, as function of global mean
    sea-level rise in meters):

    With [combined damages](#param__economics.damages.coacch_combined_slr_nonslr_damages),
    the temperature-dependent curve includes SLR impacts and the separate SLR damage term is zero.

    $$
    \href{./#var__damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{t,r}} = \href{./#var__non_slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{non-SLR},t,r}} + \href{./#var__slr_damage_costs}{\text{damages}_{\text{SLR},t,r}}
    $$

    :::mimosa.components.damages.coacch.get_constraints_temperature_dependent

    :::mimosa.components.damages.coacch.get_constraints_slr



    ## Parameters defined in this module
    - params["economics"]["damages"]["scale factor"]: Manual scaling factor to increase or decrease damages. Type: float. Default: 1. Min: -inf. Max: inf.
    - params["economics"]["damages"]["quantile"]: Damage quantile (Only used for COACCH). Type: enum. Default: 0.5. Allowed values: [0.025, 0.05, 0.16, 0.25, 0.33, 0.5, 0.67, 0.75, 0.84, 0.95, 0.975].


    """
    constraints = []
    m.damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Total regional COACCH damage costs as a fraction of gross GDP, relative to the model start. Sum of the temperature-dependent and separate sea-level-rise damage terms.",
    )
    m.damage_costs_abs = Var(
        m.t,
        m.regions,
        units=quant.unit("currency_unit"),
        doc="Total regional COACCH damage costs in currency units, calculated as the damage fraction times gross GDP.",
    )
    m.damage_scale_factor = Param(
        initialize=inputs.config("economics.damages.scale factor")
    )
    m.non_market_damage_costs_abs = Param(
        m.t, m.regions, initialize=0.0, units=quant.unit("currency_unit")
    )
    m.global_damage_costs = Var(
        m.t,
        units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"),
        doc="Global COACCH damage costs as a fraction of global gross GDP, calculated from the sum of regional damage costs in currency units.",
    )
    m.adaptation_costs = Param(
        m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("fraction_of_GDP"), initialize=0.0
    )
    m.adaptation_costs_abs = Param(
        m.t, m.regions, units=quant.unit("currency_unit"), initialize=0.0
    )
    # Total damages are sum of non-SLR and SLR damages
    constraints.extend(
        [
            RegionalEquation(
                m.damage_costs,
                lambda m, t, r: m.non_slr_damage_costs[t, r] + m.slr_damage_costs[t, r],
            ),
            RegionalEquation(
                m.damage_costs_abs,
                lambda m, t, r: m.damage_costs[t, r] * m.GDP_gross[t, r],
            ),
            GlobalEquation(
                m.global_damage_costs,
                lambda m, t: (
                    sum(m.damage_costs_abs[t, r] for r in m.regions)
                    / m.global_GDP_gross[t]
                ),
            ),
        ]
    )

    # Get constraints for temperature dependent damages
    constraints.extend(get_constraints_temperature_dependent(m, inputs))

    # Get constraints for sea-level rise damages
    constraints.extend(get_constraints_slr(m, inputs))

    return constraints

docs.title: General form of the model
docs.text:
MIMOSA is built with Pyomo, an open-source optimisation modelling package. The model combines variables and parameters with equations that calculate model outcomes and constraints that restrict the feasible solution. The selected objective module either maximises discounted welfare or minimises discounted global costs.

The following pages explain how to add variables, equations, constraints, parameters and complete model components. They focus on the conventions used in MIMOSA rather than providing a general introduction to Pyomo.

MIMOSA's shared Pyomo ConcreteModel, time and region sets, and baseline inputs are created in mimosa/base_model.py. The components listed in mimosa/model_builder.py then add their variables, parameters, equations and constraints to this shared object, which is always called m:

m = create_base_model(inputs)

The preprocessor prepares configuration and data lookup before construction. Base sets and parameters are immediately available; components add initialized parameters and variables in the explicit order in create_model. Collected constraints and the objective are attached after all declarations. There is no separate abstract-model instantiation or parameter loading from doc.

A note about file structure

After forking and cloning MIMOSA to your computer, you will find a file structure that looks like this:

MIMOSA file structure
mimosa/
├── model_builder.py # (1)!
├── base_model.py # (2)!
├── mimosa.py
├── components/ # (3)!
│   ├── emissions.py
│   ├── mitigation.py
│   └── ...
└── inputdata/
    ├── config/
    │   └── config_default.yaml # (4)!
    ├── regionalparams/
    └── data/

run.py # (5)!
  1. The model components are listed and combined in this file.
  2. Shared time, region and baseline input parameters are defined in this file.
  3. The components discussed in the Model documentation are defined in this folder.
  4. Configuration parameter types and default values are defined in this file.
  5. Example of a basic model run. Place your run files here, such that the mimosa package from this folder is used, and not a version previously installed through pip install mimosa.

For most extensions, use the following steps:

  1. Create a new component (optional, only necessary if the extension is a new module)
  2. Add new variables and constraints to the model
  3. Add new parameters and data to the model

For more advanced extensions, see Selectable modules and Model options.

docs.title: Creating model components
docs.text:
Create a new component when an extension adds a coherent part of the model with its own variables, parameters and equations. If the change only adds one or two equations to an existing subject area, it is usually clearer to add them to the existing component instead.

This page describes the most common case: adding a component that is always part of MIMOSA. This does not require changes to the configuration of the model or model options.

docs.title: Basic structure of a component
docs.text:
A component is a Python file with a function called get_constraints:

mimosa/components/new_component.py
from mimosa.common import (
    ConcreteModel,
    GlobalEquation,
    Var,
)

from mimosa.core.model_inputs import ModelInputs


def get_constraints(m: ConcreteModel, inputs: ModelInputs):
    """Calculate the square of global temperature for every time step."""

    m.temperature_squared = Var(m.t)

    return [
        GlobalEquation(
            m.temperature_squared,
            lambda m, t: m.temperature[t] ** 2,
        )
    ]

The function does three things:

  1. It adds the component's Pyomo Param, Var and related objects to the shared model m.
  2. It describes the equations and constraints that define those variables.
  3. It returns those equations and constraints, so MIMOSA can add them to the Pyomo model and use the equations in simulation mode.

Every component function receives both m and inputs. A basic component does not need to use inputs; it only needs to include it in the function definition because MIMOSA supplies it when the component is added. More advanced uses are described under Selectable modules and Model options.

GlobalEquation and RegionalEquation are used in both the Pyomo model and simulation mode. Other constraints only affect the Pyomo model. See Variables, equations and constraints for the available forms, an explanation of the lambda syntax, and complete examples of global and regional variables.

docs.title: 1. Create the component file
docs.text:
Add a Python file to mimosa/components:

mimosa/
├── model_builder.py
├── base_model.py
└── components/
    ├── emissions.py
    ├── mitigation.py
    ├── new_component.py
    └── ...

Define the component's variables, parameters, equations and constraints inside get_constraints. Variables and constraint names must be unique within MIMOSA's shared model.

When the component needs a new parameter, follow Adding parameters and data to connect the Pyomo Param to a configuration value or input file.

docs.title: 2. Add the component to MIMOSA
docs.text:
Import the component and call it in create_model in mimosa/model_builder.py:

mimosa/model_builder.py
from mimosa.components import (
    emissions,
    new_component,
    # ...
)

def create_model(inputs: ModelInputs):
    m = create_base_model(inputs)
    constraints = []
    constraints.extend(emissions.get_constraints(m, inputs))
    constraints.extend(new_component.get_constraints(m, inputs))
    # ... remaining components and constraint attachment ...

Place the call near related model components so the construction sequence remains easy to understand. References inside equation functions are evaluated after the model components have been added, so their dependencies do not normally determine the order of these calls. Direct access to another component's parameters or variables during construction does require that component to be constructed first.

That is all that is required for a component that should always be included. There is no need to add the component anywhere else. There is also no need to change config_default.yaml unless users need to choose between different versions or the component needs options while the model is being put together.

docs.title: 3. Document the component
docs.text:
Write the explanation of the component in the docstring of get_constraints. MkDocs can include this docstring directly in the model documentation:

:::mimosa.components.new_component.get_constraints

For model components, the docstring should preferably explain:

  • what the component represents;
  • the main equations and the meaning of their variables;
  • which parameters a modeller can change;
  • any numerical approximations or limitations;
  • a short usage example when the component needs special settings.

Keeping this explanation next to the equations makes it less likely that the scientific documentation and implementation drift apart.

docs.title: 4. Test the component
docs.text:
At minimum, test that:

  1. MIMOSA(params, prerun=False) can construct a model containing the new component;
  2. the expected variables and Pyomo constraints exist on model.concrete_model;
  3. returned equations can be evaluated in simulation mode.

Equation-heavy components should also compare the values of their Pyomo expressions with the values calculated in simulation mode. Keep construction tests small; only behaviour that depends on a solver needs a full optimisation run.

docs.title: More advanced components
docs.text:
Continue with:

  • Selectable modules when users should be able to choose between alternative versions of a component, or when adding a new submodule to an existing group such as damages, welfare or effort sharing;
  • Model options when a setting changes which variables or equations a component creates.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
To change MIMOSA itself or contribute to its documentation, first fork or clone the repository and open a terminal in its root directory (the directory containing pyproject.toml). We recommend using a separate conda environment:

conda create --name mimosa-dev python=3.11
conda activate mimosa-dev

Install MIMOSA in editable mode, together with the packages needed for testing and building the documentation:

python -m pip install --editable ".[test,docs]"

Editable installation means that changes to the source code are used directly; you do not need to reinstall MIMOSA after every change. If you only need one set of extra packages, use .[test] or .[docs] instead.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The following command runs the tests that do not require IPOPT:

python -m pytest tests -m "not ipopt"

After installing IPOPT, run the full test suite with:

python -m pytest tests

docs.title: Working on the documentation
docs.text:
To preview the documentation while editing it, run:

python -m mkdocs serve

MkDocs prints the local address where the preview is available and updates it when a documentation file changes. Before submitting documentation changes, also run the same strict build used by the documentation check in GitHub:

python -m mkdocs build --strict

Run these commands from the repository root so that MkDocs can find its configuration, hooks and source files.

Next: How MIMOSA is structured

docs.title: Model options
docs.text:
Model options let a component change which variables or equations it creates without introducing a separate selectable submodule. Every component receives inputs in its get_constraints(m, inputs) function and reads options through inputs.config_value. Defaults are defined once in config_default.yaml and supplied by configuration validation.

Keep an option beside the scientific parameters for the component that uses it. For example, ACCREU adaptation settings belong in economics.damages.accreu, and the sea-level-rise projection belongs in sealevelrise.

docs.title: Adding an option
docs.text:
For example, the ACCREU damage module can be constructed with no adaptation, combined adaptation, or separate adaptation by sector. Define the option under economics > damages > accreu in config_default.yaml:

mimosa/inputdata/config/config_default.yaml
economics:
  damages:
    accreu:
      adaptation:
        descr: How adaptation is represented in ACCREU
        type: enum
        values:
          - noadaptation
          - combined
          - separate
        default: separate

Defining each named option as a normal configuration entry gives it type checking, a default value and an entry in the generated parameter reference.

The component reads the option while adding its variables and equations:

def get_constraints(m, inputs):
    adaptation = inputs.config_value("economics.damages.accreu.adaptation")

    if adaptation == "sectoral":
        # Add separate adaptation variables and equations for each sector
        ...

Users can change the option before creating the model:

params = load_params()
params["economics"]["damages"]["accreu"]["adaptation"] = "sectoral"
model = MIMOSA(params)

docs.title: Model option or Pyomo parameter?
docs.text:
Use a model option when the value changes which model objects are created. For example, an option can enable a sector or choose between a combined and sector-specific set of adaptation equations.

Use a Pyomo Param for a numerical or domain assumption within equations, such as an adaptation cost, effectiveness coefficient or start year. Parameters receive values when declared on the concrete model through explicit initialization. See Adding parameters and data.

docs.title: Testing model options
docs.text:
At minimum, test that:

  1. the configuration parser accepts every documented option value;
  2. each option produces the intended variables and equations;
  3. the documented default produces the normal model structure; and
  4. unsupported option values give a clear configuration error.

Model construction with MIMOSA(params, prerun=False) is normally sufficient. Only behaviour that depends on an optimiser needs a full solver run.

docs.title: Adding parameters and data
docs.text: Parameters are values used in MIMOSA that can be changed without changing the code.

docs.title: Adding a parameter
docs.text:
Add a parameter inside a component's get_constraints(m, inputs) function. Import Param from mimosa.common and choose an initializer according to where the values come from:

from mimosa.common import Param, quant

# A fixed value, without a configuration or documentation link
m.new_param = Param(initialize=3.0)

# A value from config_default.yaml
m.PRTP = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.PRTP"))

# A value for each region, from a regional parameter CSV
m.init_capitalstock_factor = Param(
    m.regions,
    initialize=inputs.regional("economics", "init_capital_factor"),
)

# Values for each time step and region, from configured input data
m.population = Param(
    m.t, m.regions,
    initialize=inputs.time_regional("population"),
    units=quant.unit("billion people"),
)

Every component receives prepared inputs; you do not need to create it yourself. For configuration lookup, use the full path as one string, such as "economics.PRTP". The input methods also supply the documentation's source metadata in source_key. You can add an optional doc argument for a description, alongside any initializer. Regional and time-dependent values are matched to m.regions and m.t.

The three configurable input types are described below:

  1. Scalar parameters: Scalar parameters (that don't depend on region or time) are defined in the config_default.yaml file and can be modified at runtime by modifying the params dictionary. These parameters are typically used for model settings, such as the pure rate of time preference (PRTP), discount rates, etc.
  2. Regional parameters: Regional parameters (that don't depend on time) are defined in a CSV file and initialized through inputs.regional. These parameters are typically used for regional coefficients for damage functions, emissions factors, etc.
  3. Time and region dependent data: These parameters depend on both time and region, such as population and baseline GDP. Their data comes from CSV files in IAMC format.

docs.title: 1. Parameters from config file: non-regional parameters
docs.text:
Parameters read from configuration have an entry in the config_default.yaml file (located in the folder mimosa/inputdata/config/). This defines the type of the parameter (numerical, boolean, string, etc.), the default value, and the range of possible values. For example, the following entry defines the parameter economics - PRTP:

mimosa/inputdata/config/config_default.yaml
...
economics:
  PRTP:
    descr: Pure rate of time preference
    type: float
    min: 0
    max: 0.2
    default: 0.015
...

Each parameter entry in the configuration file contains the following fields:

  • descr: A description of the parameter
  • type: The type of the parameter (e.g. float, int, str, bool, ...)
  • default: The default value of the parameter
  • Optionally some extra fields depending on the type of parameter

Initialize the parameter from its configuration entry, using prepared input lookup:

m.PRTP = Param(initialize=inputs.config("economics.PRTP"))

Note that the config_default.yaml file is structured as a nested dictionary. In this case, the PRTP parameter is located within the economics group. This structure can be arbitrary and doesn't need to match the name of the component. It is purely used to structure the configuration file.

When running MIMOSA, the command params = load_params() loads all the default values from the configuration file as a nested dictionary. These values can be changed by modifying the params dictionary:

from mimosa import MIMOSA, load_params

params = load_params() 
params["economics"]["PRTP"] = 0.001
...

After this step, MIMOSA always double checks the dictionary params to check if all the parameter values have the correct type and match specifications of the configuration entry (for example, if the value is within the specified range). If not, MIMOSA will raise an error.

docs.title: Types of parameter values
docs.text:
In the example above, the PRTP has a type float. The following types are supported (especially note that for numerical values with units (values that are not dimensionless), the type quantity should be used):

Parser types float

Numerical value (float)

Extra properties:

  • min: lower bound of parameter (default: -inf)
  • max: upper bound of parameter (default: +inf)

Example usage:

time:
  dt:
    default: 5
    descr: Initial timestep length in years
    max: 20
    min: 0.5
    type: float

int

Numerical value (integer)

Extra properties:

  • min: lower bound of parameter (default: -inf)
  • max: upper bound of parameter (default: +inf)

Example usage:

time:
  start:
    default: 2025
    descr: Year in which the model starts
    max: 2100
    min: 1900
    type: int

bool

Boolean value (true or false).

Example usage:

economics:
  damages:
    ignore damages:
      default: false
      descr: Flag to not take into account the damages in the GDP (but damages are calculated)
      type: bool

str

String value

enum

Enum (discrete list of options)

Extra properties:

  • values: list of allowed values

Example usage:

SSP:
  default: SSP2
  descr: SSP, used for population, baseline GDP and baseline emissions
  type: enum
  values:
  - SSP1
  - SSP2
  - SSP3
  - SSP4
  - SSP5

quantity

Quantity (value with unit). The provided value will be converted to the unit, if possible.

For example, if the unit of a parameter is GtCO2, and the parameter value provided by the user is "1000 MtCO2", the value will be converted automatically to "1 GtCO2". The value passed to MIMOSA will therefore be 1, and not 1000. If the user provides "1000 US$", MIMOSA will raise an exception, as this cannot be converted to GtCO2.

Extra properties:

  • unit: Unit of the quantity

Example usage:

economics:
  MAC:
    gamma:
      default: 2887 USD2010/tCO2
      descr: Calibration level of the MAC (carbon price for 100% reduction)
      type: quantity
      unit: currency_unit/emissionsrate_unit

list

List of values. The values are also parsed individually, depending on the parser type given in the property values.

Extra properties:

  • values: parser information for the values. For example, the values can be int, float, values with units, etc.

Example usage:

regionsmappings:
  default:
  - conversiontable: inputdata/regions/IMAGE26_COACCH.csv
    regionstype1: IMAGE26
    regionstype2: COACCH
  - conversiontable: inputdata/regions/IMAGE26_ADRICE2010.csv
    regionstype1: IMAGE26
    regionstype2: ADRICE2010
  - conversiontable: inputdata/regions/IMAGE26_ADRICE2012.csv
    regionstype1: IMAGE26
    regionstype2: ADRICE2012
  descr: List of region types and their conversion tables. Only used for regional parameters,
    not for aggregating or disaggregating variables or other output.
  type: list
  values:
    descr: Dictionary with keys `regionstype1`, `regionstype2` and `conversiontable`.
    type: dict

dict

Dictionary with keys and values. The values are also parsed individually, depending on the parser type given in the property values.

Extra properties:

  • values: parser information for the values. For example, the values can be int, float, values with units, etc.
  • keys: parser information for the keys

Example usage:

time:
  periods:
    default:
      2050: 10
    descr: Optional timestep changes, mapping each change year to the timestep length
      in years used after that year
    keys:
      max: 2300
      min: 1901
      type: int
    type: dict
    values:
      max: 20
      min: 0.5
      type: float

datasource

Data source for a variable. It's a dictionary with the keys variable, unit, scenario, model, and file.

Example usage:

input:
  variables:
    GDP:
      default:
        file: inputdata/data/data_IMAGE_SSP_updated.csv
        model: IMAGE 3.4
        scenario: '{SSP}-Baseline'
        unit: currency_unit
        variable: GDP|PPP
      descr: Data source of GDP
      type: datasource

filepath

Filepath value. Currently exactly the same as the string type.

str_or_num_or_plain_dict

Either a string or a dictionary. The keys/values of the dictionary are not checked or parsed separately.

docs.title: 2. Regional parameters
docs.text:
The configuration file can be used to set scalar parameters. However, some parameters are regional. These are created like:

m.new_regional_param = Param(
    m.regions, initialize=inputs.regional("newparamgroup", "newparam1")
)

Initializing their value is done in three steps:

  1. Create a CSV file with a column region and the columns with regional parameter values you want to use:

    In the folder mimosa/inputdata/regionalparams/, create a new CSV file:

    mimosa
│   ...
│
└─── inputdata
    └─── config
        │   config_default.yaml
    └─── regionalparams
        │   economics.csv
        |   mac.csv 
        |   newfile.csv
        |   ...

    This file should have at least a column region and one (or more) columns for the regional values:

    mimosa/inputdata/regionalparams/newfile.csv

    region newparam1 newparam2 ... CAN 1.992 2.317 ... USA 2.035 1.745 ... ... ...

    Note that this file can contain multiple columns (for multiple regional parameters). It is good practice to group the parameter values when the parameters are somehow related with each other.
